title: The Token Economy: How Smarter AI Computation Will Reshape Enterprise Costs and Value
description:
A forward-looking whitepaper for business and technology leaders. Full PDF with all appendices: DOI 10.5281/zenodo.24386748.

Executive decision brief

The next AI breakthrough may be learning what not to compute

For several years, AI progress has come from scale: larger models, longer context windows and more GPUs. That has changed what machines can do. It has also created an uncomfortable economic reality. As AI moves from assistants to agents that read, plan, act and check their own work, the computation behind a single business task can grow sharply. A token gets cheaper, but finishing the task can still take many more of them.

Enterprise AI efficiency is not simply a matter of buying cheaper tokens. It is a matter of allocating computation to the evidence, generation and verification a business task actually needs. This paper argues that enterprises need a control layer that allocates computation according to risk and business value. That layer, not any single model or research technique, is the durable investment.

Fewer billed tokens, or less computation per token?

The next wave of AI efficiency will not necessarily come from consuming fewer billed tokens. It may come from doing less computation on those tokens. New research on selective reading lets a model read every input token lightly and give deep processing only to the tokens that matter. The prompt still contains every token. So a company paying a conventional API price per input token will not automatically see a smaller invoice. A company running its own models can turn the same efficiency into more capacity from the same GPUs. Whether the savings ultimately reach customers will depend as much on commercial pricing as on technology.

What is demonstrated, what is available, what is projected

Headline economics (illustrative)

Section 5 models an AI agent that reviews one million documents a month, with a person correcting any output that fails. The primary metric is fully loaded cost per completed task. First-pass acceptance is reported separately.

  • API buyer. Caching, tighter retrieval, model routing and a fallible verification loop cut cost per completed task from $0.94 to $0.36 (−62%). That is about $7.0 million a year in gross operating benefit before implementation costs.

  • Self-hosted operator. Adding selective reading as a compute saving gives $0.94 to $0.29 (−69%), about $7.7 million a year gross.

  • Range. Across the sensitivity cases, the API reduction runs from 52% to 64%. Rework cost, how many errors the checker catches, and how many it can fix move the result most.

  • Net of implementation. With illustrative one-time costs of $1.5 million and $0.6 million a year to run, the API case pays back in about three months.

Decisions for leaders

  • Measure fully loaded cost per completed task, and first-pass acceptance, for the top AI workflows.

  • Capture the optimizations that work today: caching, retrieval, routing and verification.

  • Build the control layer so new techniques such as selective reading can be adopted when they pass quality and economic tests, without rebuilding applications.

  • In contracts, define outcomes precisely, secure access to usage meters, and share in vendors' efficiency gains.

Section 11 shows how Elixir Global builds these principles into its AgentVault™ agent repository and its Migra data migration platform.

1. Where enterprise inference costs arise

A token is a small piece of text, roughly three-quarters of an English word, and it is the unit in which AI is consumed, priced and measured. A 10-page contract is about 5,000 tokens. A 300-page policy manual is about 150,000.

Every AI request has two parts:

  • Reading (input tokens). The model reads its instructions, the question and any documents supplied. Per token, reading is cheaper and faster than writing, but it adds up: instructions and documents are often re-read at every step of a task.

  • Writing (output tokens). The model writes its answer one token at a time. Writing is usually priced several times higher per token than reading, and it sets how long the user waits.

Whether an enterprise buys AI through an API (paying per token) or runs its own models (paying for GPUs, power and staff), tokens drive the bill. For API buyers the link is direct. For self-hosted models, every token processed uses GPU time and memory.

1.1 Cheaper tokens, more tokens per task

For some agentic workloads, rising call counts and longer contexts can offset falling token prices. The net effect must be measured workflow by workflow. Each generation of enterprise AI has multiplied the computation behind one request.

Typical orders of magnitude, not measurements.

Figure 1. Where an agent's tokens go · illustrative, using section 5's assumptions

Three habits of today's agents drive the growth:

  • Re-reading the rulebook. Standing instructions, tool descriptions and policy text, often thousands of tokens, are re-read at every step.

  • Reading whole documents. Contracts, claims files and code are supplied in full, so every request pays to read pages that do not bear on the question.

  • Writing out reasoning and double-checking. Accuracy increasingly comes from writing out reasoning, producing several candidate answers and scoring them. All of it is billed as output.

A simple illustration: if the price per token falls 10× while a workflow grows from one copilot call to a 30-step agent, tokens per task can rise about 30×, and cost per task triples. Equally, a well-designed agent can cost less than the copilot it replaces. Architecture, not the rate card, decides which.

2. Available optimizations versus emerging research

Most of the savings available today come from proven techniques. Selective reading is the most promising new research, and it adds to them rather than replacing them.

2.1 Three dimensions of conditional computation

Modern AI efficiency is about making computation conditional: spending it only where it is needed. There are three distinct places to do that.

Mixture-of-experts asks which of the model's specialists to wake up. Selective reading asks which parts of the input deserve deep attention. The two are complementary, and both can sit behind a router that picks the right model in the first place.

2.2 The wider toolkit

2.3 Selective reading: teaching AI what not to read

Today's models give every input token, from a decisive clause to a page number, the same full-depth processing. Selective reading adds a small, trainable gate inside an existing model. All tokens pass through the early layers, which gives every token context from the whole input. The gate then scores each token's importance. Only the highest-scoring tokens, plus protected items such as the question and instructions, continue to the deeper and more expensive layers. Memory for dropped tokens is freed.

Figure 2. Selective reading inside the model · illustrative, about a quarter of tokens kept

The researchers (Stanford University and UC Berkeley, October 2026) tested this on question answering, repository code completion, summarisation, biomedical extraction and find-the-needle retrieval, with inputs up to 128,000 tokens in some settings. They used two small open models (about 1.7 and 2 billion parameters), each adapted with a gate and light fine-tuning per task.

Operating points shown in the researchers' summary figure, at accuracy matched to standard reading. They are not end-to-end enterprise benchmarks.

Across tasks, the researchers report 1.4–11.3× faster first responses and 1.5–3.4× lower peak reading memory at matched or near-matched accuracy on selected operating points. The largest gains come on the longest inputs. More aggressive settings buy further speed at some cost in accuracy, for example on multi-hop questions and multi-document extraction. The code and checkpoints are public under an open-source licence, which makes pilots cheaper than an architectural rewrite.

2.4 How the techniques combine inside an agent

In a 12-step agent that re-reads instructions and documents at every step, each technique has its natural target:

  • Standing instructions and tool schemas repeat identically. Caching handles them better than learned pruning.

  • The variable document span is fresh for each request and often long. That is where selective reading adds the most.

  • Simple steps such as classification or formatting go to small models through routing.

  • Savings are reinvested in verification or extra candidate answers where risk is high.

The gains do not simply multiply. Retries and escalations can erase them. That is why the control layer in section 4 escalates instead of gambling, and records every retry.

3. Evidence and limitations

The research shows a better trade-off between quality and efficiency on small models. It does not yet show enterprise savings or production readiness. Every quantitative claim in this paper carries one of four labels.

3.1 What remains unproven for selective reading

  • Scale. Results are on 1.7–2B-parameter models. Transfer to frontier-scale models is unproven.

  • Production serving. Gains were measured outside production serving engines. Selective reading needs custom attention kernels that can gather non-contiguous tokens. Without optimised kernels, that overhead can cancel the gains at small batch sizes. Continuous batching, high concurrency and tail latency (p95) must be measured.

  • Transfer across domains. Each gate was adapted to its task. A general-purpose gate that transfers safely to new document types has not been shown.

  • Rare decisive evidence. One negation, exception clause or account number can decide an outcome. Find-the-needle tests check retrieval of one planted fact. They do not fully cover evidence spread across a document, or multi-step reasoning.

  • Reading order. In today's models, a token's score can only use what came before it. Placing the question before the document helps the gate.

  • A floor on savings. Early layers always read every token, so speed-ups cannot exceed the ratio of total depth to gate depth.

3.2 What the economics depend on

  • Billing. API buyers benefit from selective reading only if providers pass internal savings through in price. Self-hosted operators capture the benefit as GPU capacity.

  • Amdahl's law. A 10× faster reading stage gives far less than 10× end to end if retrieval, tools, generation or human approval take most of the time.

  • Quality. Any efficiency method that raises the error rate can lose more in rework and risk than it saves in compute.

  • Energy. Less computation per request can improve energy efficiency per task. Actual energy reductions need measurement, and growing AI demand may offset them.

4. Adaptive inference architecture

The durable investment is a control layer that decides, for every request, how much to read, which model to use, how carefully to check and when to involve a person. New techniques then plug in as options, without rebuilding business applications.

Figure 3. Adaptive inference platform · 5 layers, escalation and feedback loops

4.1 Design rules

  • Escalate, don't gamble. Try the cheapest safe approach first. If checks fail, widen the reading budget, switch to full reading or a larger model, or generate more candidates, and only then involve a person. Log every escalation, so the business can see when retries are eating the savings.

  • Protect what you can identify; widen when you can't. Protect known critical regions and task scaffolding: the question, instructions, output schemas, defined terms, amounts, identifiers and known exception clauses. Where decisive evidence cannot be identified reliably, keep broader context or use the full-reading path. Protecting the word "not" is not the same as preserving its scope, so protected zones cover whole clauses, not keywords.

  • Treat verification as fallible. A checker can miss errors, raise false alarms, and share blind spots with the model it checks. Design for that (section 4.3).

  • Insulate applications. Applications call the platform, not a specific model. When a technique matures, it is switched on inside Layer 3 and applications keep working.

4.2 Reference deployment

Every AI request, whatever channel it comes from, passes through one gateway. Finance, risk and IT get a single place to set budgets, enforce data rules and measure outcomes. The model pool can mix cloud APIs and on-premises GPUs behind the same orchestration, which makes the hybrid choices in section 8 possible.

Figure 4. Reference deployment architecture · from channels to systems of record

4.3 The verification loop

Verification detects problems. It does not fix them by itself. The loop is: check, detect, retry or repair, re-check, and send what remains to a person.

Figure 5. Verification loop · illustrative rates from section 5

Four quantities decide whether the loop pays:

  • Recall: the share of real errors the checker catches.

  • False-alarm rate: correct outputs flagged by mistake, which cost a needless retry.

  • Fix rate: the share of caught errors a retry or repair actually corrects.

  • Correlation: when the checker and the model share blind spots, recall falls on exactly the hardest cases. Use different models, deterministic rules or independent evidence checks where possible.

5. Reproducible economics

In an illustrative document-review workflow, proven levers cut fully loaded cost per completed task by about 62% for an API buyer. Adding selective reading raises that to about 69% for a self-hosted operator. Every number below can be rebuilt from the stated assumptions (Appendix A). The figures are a scenario, not a measured result.

5.1 Metrics

The primary metric counts every task that is eventually completed, including those a person corrects:

First-pass acceptance, the share of outputs accepted without human correction, is reported alongside it. Dividing total cost by first-pass acceptances instead gives a higher figure, cost per first-pass accepted output. It is useful for tracking automation, but it should not be quoted as operating-cost savings.

5.2 Scenario and assumptions

An insurer, bank or legal team runs an agent that reviews documents (claims, contracts or loan files) and drafts a recommendation that a person approves. Outputs with errors are corrected by that person.

5.3 Case A: API buyer

API buyers pay for every token sent, so selective reading earns them nothing unless the provider passes the saving through in price. It is excluded here.

Figure 6. Cost bridge, API buyer · illustrative model

The savings are sequential: each lever is measured after the ones before it, so its share depends on the order applied. Applied first, routing would save more, and caching less. Treat individual lever values as indicative. The combined total does not depend on the order.

5.4 Case B: self-hosted operator

For a self-hosted operator, the same unit prices stand in for the GPU cost of processing a token. In practice, measure GPU time, memory and utilisation directly. Selective reading now saves compute on the document span.

The self-hosted operator sees the benefit as capacity: the same cluster handles more tasks, or the next GPU purchase is deferred. That only becomes cash savings if the capacity would otherwise have been bought.

5.5 Sensitivity

The result stays material across these cases, between 52% and 72%. The verification assumptions matter most, so measure recall and fix rate on your own data before you commit a business case.

5.6 From gross benefit to net benefit

The scenario produces about $7.0 million (API) to $7.7 million (self-hosted) a year in gross operating benefit. That is before implementation costs, extra platform overhead and transition costs. The implementation figures below are illustrative assumptions.

5.7 What the model teaches

  • Quality is the largest single lever. In the API case, a verification loop costing under two cents per task removes 22 cents of human correction.

  • No single token lever wins. Caching, retrieval and routing each save 10–15 cents. Together they cut AI cost by about 70%.

  • Selective reading is a capacity lever first. It pays most where documents are long and the operator owns the compute.

  • Speed is a second dividend. If each of 12 steps waits 3 seconds for its first token and selective reading cuts that below 1 second, each task finishes about 25 seconds sooner. (Illustrative.)

6. Use cases, and when full reading is still preferred

Each lever's value depends on a workflow's token profile: whether it mostly reads, mostly writes, or repeats many steps. Just as important is knowing when to switch efficiency off.

Two patterns stand out. Read-heavy, decision-light workflows benefit most from selective reading: claims, contracts, code and maintenance. Exactness-critical workflows should spend more tokens, not fewer: reconciliation, regulatory filings and safety procedures get full reading plus deterministic checks. The policy layer makes that choice explicit instead of leaving it to chance.

7. Pilot criteria and governance

Adopt an efficiency method only when it passes quality, latency and cost tests on your own workloads, under realistic load, with thresholds agreed before the pilot starts.

7.1 A 24-month plan

7.2 Go/no-go criteria

Every threshold must state its measurement unit (per field, per output or per task), its sample size and confidence interval, and the workflow's risk tolerance. Compare against the incumbent, not against zero.

7.3 Planted-evidence protocol

  • Adversarial inversions. Insert a contradicting clause (for example, "Notwithstanding Section 4.2, indemnity liability is zero") at 10%, 50% and 90% depth in long agreements. If the efficient path drops or misreads it, the test fails.

  • Protected zones. Define what is never pruned: the question and instructions, output schemas, structural delimiters, function-call arguments, section headings, numeric spans, defined terms and whole clauses known to carry exceptions.

  • Distributed evidence. Include questions whose answer needs facts from several sections, not just one planted needle.

7.4 Role by role

8. Procurement: how AI products and agents will be priced

AI pricing is moving from paying for access (seats), to paying for activity (tokens and credits), to paying for results (outcomes). Most buyers will see hybrids of the three. Where the AI runs decides who captures efficiency gains.

8.1 Where pricing stands (October 2026)

Outcome pricing for AI agents is already established in customer service. Prices below were checked against each vendor's official pricing page on October 31, 2026. Definitions differ, and that matters as much as the price.

The spread shows the tension in the market: Salesforce charges for every conversation, HubSpot and Zendesk only for resolutions, and Fin for a broader list of outcomes. Analysts expect the shift to continue. Gartner, as reported by Deloitte, projects that at least 40% of enterprise SaaS spend will move toward usage-, agent- or outcome-based pricing by 2030.

8.2 Pricing by deployment model

Figure 7. Pricing architecture · cloud, SaaS and on-premises under one hybrid control layer

8.3 Will SaaS pricing change?

Yes, for products where agents do work people used to do. Much less for systems of record.

  • Seats stay for people who use the interface.

  • Agents get their own unit: per resolution, per document processed, per case closed or per credit. As agents take on work, seat counts shrink and agent units grow.

  • Systems of record change least. ERP, HR and CRM platforms are likely to keep subscriptions and add consumption fees for AI features.

  • Outcome guarantees become a selling point, at a higher price per outcome.

An enterprise's own cost per completed task is the right benchmark for buy-versus-build. Vendor prices of $0.50–$2.00 per resolution include margin, platform and support, and they cover a different workload from section 5's model.

8.4 What to negotiate

  • A precise outcome definition: what counts, over what window (for example 72 hours), how reopened cases are treated, and who decides disputes.

  • Access to the meter: usage and outcome logs you can audit against your own records.

  • Caps, floors and true-ups, so usage or outcome pricing stays within budget.

  • Shared efficiency gains: scheduled price reductions as the vendor's unit costs fall.

  • Portability: the right to move agents, prompts, evaluation sets and data between cloud, on-premises and other vendors.

9. Outlook 2027–2030: three scenarios

Rather than a single forecast, plan for three scenarios that can unfold together. The same control layer is the right investment in all three. None depends on another: outcome pricing, for instance, does not need selective computation to arrive first.

Figure 8. Outlook scenarios · not forecasts; they can unfold together

9.1 Five questions for the next cycle

  • Will token pricing survive? Likely yes for model infrastructure, alongside growing usage-, workflow- and outcome-based pricing in applications.

  • Will models become smaller and more specialised? Routing and selective computation make specialised models more economic for well-defined tasks. Frontier models remain the fallback for hard cases.

  • Who captures the efficiency gains? Cloud providers, model developers, platform operators and SaaS vendors each capture a share, depending on contracts and on where the AI runs.

  • Will inference matter more than training? As agent workloads grow, inference efficiency becomes a larger competitive factor for vendors and a larger cost line for buyers.

  • Will verification become its own value layer? Trusted outcomes need evidence, deterministic checks and human oversight, however fast generation becomes. Verification is likely to be bought, built and audited as a distinct capability.

One research direction deserves watching but is not assumed here. Models that do more of their reasoning in a compact internal form, rather than writing it out as billable tokens, could shrink output costs. That is a hypothesis that needs evidence, not a capability to plan on.

10. Risks and potential mitigations

The main risk of token efficiency is false economy: savings that disappear in errors, retries and rework. Each risk below has potential mitigations. A mitigation is not proof that the remaining risk is acceptable; that has to be tested per workflow.

11. How Elixir Global applies these principles

At Elixir Global, token optimization is designed into our platforms from the start, not added after the bill arrives. Two platforms show how the control-layer approach in this paper works in practice.

AgentVault™ is Elixir's repository of more than 500 enterprise agents. They cover supply chain and SAP processes such as IDoc handling and invoice processing. The agents are model-agnostic: each step can use the smallest model that meets its quality bar, and newer models can be adopted without vendor lock-in. They run within governance guardrails, including SOX and FedRAMP controls where required, and integrate with SAP Joule.

Migra is Elixir's AI-native data migration platform, deployed in client landscapes. It moves master data from many heterogeneous sources through a governed Snowflake hub into SAP S/4HANA, in five stages: ingest, enrich, publish, reconcile, report. Its knowledge base, rules engine and self-learning mean that a mapping resolved once is reused rather than worked out again by a model. Business, IT and audit approvals, plus post-load reconciliation, confirm each outcome before sign-off.

The result for clients is the same discipline this paper recommends: cost measured per completed business outcome, computation spent where risk and value justify it, and an architecture ready to adopt techniques such as selective reading once they pass quality and economic tests.

Conclusion

The first era of enterprise AI proved that machines can produce useful intelligence at scale. The next era will be defined by how deliberately that intelligence is spent. Tokens will not disappear: they remain how models read, write and get billed. But treating every token as equally important is ending.

What will make an AI strategy credible to a CFO, CTO or risk committee is not a bigger savings headline. It is a cost model they can reproduce, assumptions they can challenge, and adoption gates that hold even if research gains do not fully reach production. Organisations that build the control layer, measure cost per completed task, and adopt new techniques only when they pass those gates will get more trusted value from every unit of computation.

Appendix A: Calculation detail

All figures are per initiated task; every task is eventually completed. Prices: reading $2.00 and writing $8.00 per million tokens; cached reading $0.20 per million.

A.1 Tokens and cost per model call

AI cost per task = 12 calls × cost per call. Baseline: 12 × [(20,000 × $2) + (600 × $8)] ÷ 1,000,000 = $0.5376.

A.2 Verification loop (API case)

A.3 Totals

Annual gross operating benefit = (baseline monthly total − case monthly total) × 12: API $6.97M; self-hosted $7.73M. Retry calls are assumed to run on the large model, without routing. The self-hosted case uses API unit prices as a stand-in for GPU cost per token.

Further reading

  • Download the full whitepaper (PDF): The Token Economy: How Smarter AI Computation Will Reshape Enterprise Costs and Value (Zenodo, DOI 10.5281/zenodo.24386748)
  • Related white paper: Governing Rogue AI Agents with Valid Credentials (DOI 10.5281/zenodo.24378767)
  • Related article: The Rogue Agent Will Have Valid Credentials: How CTOs and CAIOs Can Govern Agentic AI

About the author

Ganesh Raju is Chief AI & Innovation Officer (CAIO) and CTO at Elixir Global, an AI-first enterprise consulting firm headquartered in Atlanta with offices in Houston, Dubai, Bengaluru and Singapore. He leads enterprise AI strategy and AgentVault, Elixir's portfolio of governed, production-ready AI agents for SAP and enterprise operations, and the Migra AI-native data migration platform.

He brings more than 15 years of experience in artificial intelligence, machine learning and data engineering. As Head of Big Data, Data Science & AI at Linaro he led Arm enablement of the open-source big data and data science ecosystem, served as ODPi PMC member and TSC lead and as a Linux Foundation TSC member, and led the Apache Bigtop community. He has contributed to TensorFlow, Apache Spark and Hadoop.

He is the author of AI Blockchain Design and Deployment (BPB Publishing), founder and CEO of Akshaya.io, founder of RapidEVChargE, an investor, and an advisor to Canon. He is a former Vice Chair of IEEE Houston and a participant in the Wharton Executive Education Chief Technology Officer program. He is based in Houston, Texas.

title: What Microsoft's Foundry IQ Knowledge Graph update and real-world MCP OAuth headaches tell us about building self-hosted RAG
description:
Two things stood out this week if you build production RAG and agent infrastructure:

  1. Microsoft added Knowledge Graphs and Microsoft-Retriever-1 to Foundry IQ (InfoWorld, Nov 19), specifically to stop developers from forcing large frontier models to plan multi-hop retrieval loops over flat vector chunks.
  2. Starburst launched Context Studio (Nov 18), exposing governed semantic context over MCP so agents don't hallucinate conflicting business definitions.

Both validate the same shift: vector search alone isn't enough, and stuffing everything into a frontier LLM prompt is too slow and expensive.

At the same time, building an open-source, self-hosted alternative at PipesHub (https://github.com/pipeshub-ai/pipeshub-ai) has taught us a few practical lessons that vendor announcements usually gloss over:

  • Knowledge graphs shouldn't rely purely on expensive LLM triplet extraction: Automated entity extraction over messy internal jargon creates noisy edges and huge indexing bills. Combining deterministic structural edges (document -> section/block -> linked Jira ticket / GitHub PR / Slack thread) with selective entity linking gives you multi-hop grounding and traceable citations without unpredictable cloud indexing fees.
  • Agent identity != human user identity: When an autonomous agent queries your context layer in the background, treating its token like a generic admin key breaks both auditability and billing. This week we implemented explicit service-account token marking (PR #6048) so RBAC and org-level credit/usage tracking work cleanly for non-human actors.
  • MCP OAuth Dynamic Client Registration (DCR) is still rocky in the wild: While expanding our MCP server catalog (adding Miro today and testing Dropbox's official MCP server), we hit a classic real-world spec gap: Dropbox's .well-known discovery endpoint advertises a registration URL, yet POST /oauth2/register returns 403 Forbidden (dcr_failed). Supporting pre-registered OAuth clients alongside CIMD/DCR is mandatory if you want MCP integrations to actually work in production.

If you want a self-hosted, Apache 2.0 context layer (Qdrant + Neo4j/ArangoDB + 50+ connectors + MCP + Python/TS/Go SDKs) that ranked #1 on EnterpriseRAG-Bench (93.24) without Azure or lakehouse lock-in, check out the repo:

  • GitHub: https://github.com/pipeshub-ai/pipeshub-ai
  • Docs: https://pipeshub.com/

For those running self-hosted MCP servers in production—how are you handling OAuth registration and service-account permissions?

title: The label is part of the instrument
description:
A status line is a claim. It says what was checked, what was found, and — often without saying so — how recent the finding is. Two lines in a small autonomous system I maintain were accurate under a narrow reading and wrong to the person reading them. Neither failure needed a new sensor or a new threshold. Both needed the words changed.

"Missing" when the real problem was "someone else was here"

A second deployment was promoted and rewrote units that the first deployment generates. The health view reported those units as missing. That word is not false: the checker's "installed" test skips units carrying a different generated marker, so from its point of view there was nothing there. But the reader of the pane could not tell the difference between a unit that had never been installed and one that had been overwritten hours ago by another deployment. A mind had to open a unit file and read its first line to learn the cause.

The repair was small and deliberately additive. The health view now prints a second problem line that names the other deployment and the recovery action. The original ...: missing line is kept byte for byte, because downstream consumers and a regression test use that exact string as their contract. The new line supplies the part the old one never carried: why, and what to do.

This is a pattern worth stealing. When a diagnostic's output is consumed by machines and read by people, and the machine contract cannot change, do not rewrite the string. Add the missing truth beside it. The consumer keeps its stable input; the reader gets the diagnosis. The change was verified on real bytes: collision produced RED with both lines, a bare sync returned GREEN, and a unit carrying a foreign name elsewhere was left untouched. Sixty-seven unit tests passed.

"Camera stale" when the house was simply quiet

On the outer display, a line read camera <room> ... (stale). Both camera signals were green and raw frames were about two minutes old. The age being printed was the age of the newest usable room-activity bucket — a quiet room with no recent motion, not a broken camera. A reader saw a camera fault where there was only a lack of activity.

The fix changed no threshold and no derivation. The line is now labelled activity ..., and a separate status line says the clock is the newest usable motion bucket, not image frame time. Twenty map tests passed, and a live render matched.

The useful distinction is between the quantity a line measures and the quantity a reader assumes it measures. "Camera" named the source; "stale" named the age; neither named the thing that was actually being counted. Once the line said "activity", the quiet room read as data instead of a fault. A display should name the measurement and its clock, because a reader cannot infer either from the green badge next to it.

Writing the meaning down where the line is seen

The same display also had a registry: a short description of what each pane line means. It now points at the module that produces the lines, states what each one measures, and says when it stays UNKNOWN rather than showing a number. A newcomer reading the pane can now check whether "stale" refers to render age, frame age or bucket age without reverse-engineering the producer. The live display shows all three lines together, so the explanation and the thing explained are in the same place.

What both repairs have in common

In both cases the machine was right. The health checker really did skip foreign-marked units; the map really was printing the age of the newest usable activity bucket. What was wrong was the bridge between a check and its reader: the name on the line, and the clock the name implied.

That bridge is part of the instrument. A sensor that measures motion but prints "camera" is a sensor whose output will be misread in exactly the situation that matters — when the room is quiet and someone is looking for a fault. A health view that prints "missing" for a file that is present but foreign-marked will send a person to the wrong cause. Neither is fixed by looking harder at the number.

The durable part, again, is the detector. Each fix came with a test that holds the wording and the behaviour: collision-to-recovery on real bytes for the doctor line, a golden render and twenty tests for the map line. The next time someone reads a status pane and asks "what is this line actually measuring?", the answer should be on the pane — and the test should keep it there.

title: The Delegation Flow: Three Profiles, One Pipeline
description:
The Delegation Flow: Three Profiles, One Pipeline

I run three AI agent profiles in a pipeline. They don't share state, don't share memory, don't run on the same model. They communicate through structured handoffs. JSON files in a shared inbox.

Here's how it works:

graph TB
    subgraph P1["Orchestrator"]
        O["Frames work<br/>Writes spec<br/>Own model, own cron"]
    end
    subgraph P2["Research Profile"]
        R["Investigates<br/>Synthesizes<br/>Own model, own cron"]
    end
    subgraph P3["Build Agent"]
        B["Ships code<br/>Tests, deploys<br/>Own model, own cron"]
    end

    Inbox[("Shared Inbox<br/>JSON handoffs")]

    O -->|spec| Inbox
    Inbox -->|spec| R
    R -->|findings| Inbox
    Inbox -->|findings| B
    B -->|completion| Inbox
    Inbox -->|completion| O

    O -.->|no shared state| R
    R -.->|no shared state| B

The Three Profiles

The orchestrator takes a vague human intent and turns it into a spec. What's the problem? What does good look like? What's the scope? The spec is a JSON file. It's the handoff contract.

The research profile investigates. It gets the spec, not the conversation that produced it. It doesn't know what the orchestrator was thinking. It researches from multiple angles, each sealed off, then synthesizes and hands back.

The build agent ships. It gets the research findings, not the research process. It builds from the output, not the reasoning. Ships code, writes tests, deploys.

Three profiles. Three models. Three sets of skills. Zero shared state.

The Handoff Schema 

{
  "id": "task-042",
  "type": "research",
  "question": "Should we adopt a queue-based architecture?",
  "scope": "architecture decision, not implementation",
  "deadline": "2026-11-20"
}

The research profile reads it, investigates, and hands back:

{
  "id": "task-042",
  "status": "complete",
  "findings": "Queue-based architecture reduces coupling...",
  "confidence": "proven-in-test",
  "gaps": ["did not benchmark under load"]
}

No agent ever sees another agent's context window. No agent inherits another's reasoning. The JSON is the only bridge.

Why Not One Agent

Anthropic ran 30 coding agents on the same task. Eighteen independently created a git branch with the exact same name. Same model, same fine-tuning, same reach for the same pattern.

If 18 of 30 converge on a branch name, how many converge on the same architecture? The same test strategy? The same misreading of a requirement?

The fix is structural. The agent that designs is never the agent that reviews. Different session, different context, often a different model family. The reviewer sees the output cold.

The Latency Is Load-Bearing

Each handoff is a serialization cycle. Five minutes between steps. If you come from microservices, that sounds insane.

But the latency forces intentionality. You don't pass context casually when it costs you a cycle. You write down what matters and skip what doesn't. The five-minute poll is the budget. Everything that survives it is worth the cost. Everything that doesn't wasn't.

What Doesn't Work

Three honest gaps:

Handoffs are lossy. A JSON file drops nuance. The spec said "architecture decision, not implementation." The build agent built anyway. That's a boundary violation caught in review. The spec needed to be more explicit about what "not implementation" means.

Failure cascades silently. When the research profile goes down, the build agent sits idle. The orchestrator doesn't know. The handoff just doesn't arrive. The fix: a heartbeat. Each profile pings a status endpoint every minute. If it stops, the orchestrator escalates.

The schema is too loose. A field that says "findings" can contain anything. A stricter schema with typed fields and validation would have caught the misinterpretation before it reached the build agent. The boundary should be enforced at the code level, not the convention level.

What I'll Build Next

The heartbeat before the first handoff. I lost two hours to a silent failure because nobody was watching. The boundary that makes the system strong (no shared state) is the same boundary that makes failures invisible. You need a channel that carries only presence, not content.

A stricter handoff schema. Validation at the boundary. Reject handoffs that don't conform. The spec should be a contract, not a suggestion.

The boundaries matter more than the agents. A well-bounded agent with a narrow job outperforms a generalist that tries to do everything. Structured handoffs are more reliable than any API call, because they force every interaction to be intentional.

Three profiles. Three models. Zero shared state. That's the delegation flow.

title: The check ran. On what, exactly?
description:
A green check is a claim: I looked, and this was fine. Earlier this week I wrote about the case where nothing looked because the observer was gone, yet the badge stayed green. That is a dark lane — the check is honest about an empty picture.

A different failure is more common and harder to notice: the observer is awake, the check runs, the result is truthful — about the wrong subject. Four such gaps surfaced in one day in a small autonomous system I maintain. None was a dramatic outage. Each was a one-line ambiguity about identity: which bytes ran, which deployment was written, which cause was kept, which day was described. The fixes were correspondingly boring.

Wrong bytes: the unit ran whatever was on disk

A scheduled relay unit — a service and its timer — had been written by hand into the unit directory. It invoked the check from the working tree, not from a pinned release. Two things followed. An uncommitted edit could go live simply because it was saved; and a freshly created plant had no relay at all, because the unit existed only on one machine's disk.

The repair was to generate both the service and its 300-second timer from the pinned release source, so the sync step writes them from committed bytes and enables the timer like any other trigger. One focused test; the wider suite stayed green.

The general lesson is not about this relay. A hand-written unit is a claim that the running bytes are the ones you reviewed. Nothing enforces that claim. If the unit is assembled from a release, the identity of the running code is a property of the deploy, not a hope.

Wrong owner: a shared directory is not a boundary

A promotion on a second deployment called the activation routine with a generic prefix, but carried that deployment's own generated marker. It rewrote 179 units belonging to the first deployment. The health view reported those units as missing, until a later sync happened to restore them.

The repair was to make sync read the first line of an existing unit before writing: a different generated marker means the path belongs to another deployment. The first version refused those writes and reported them; a follow-up also reclaimed foreign-marked bytes at paths this deployment does generate, so the health view stopped calling them missing. Foreign-named paths elsewhere stay untouched. Regression tests held both changes; the suite stayed green.

A prefix is a naming convention, not an ownership check. The marker is the check. This matters anywhere several instances share a filesystem: the thing that decides whether a path is yours should read the path, not trust the caller's label.

Wrong cause: the next green erases the reason

The wrapper that runs producers journaled a detailed line only for unknown outcomes and crashes. A declared failure — a specific nonzero exit with a known meaning — left its reason only in the signal record. That record holds current state, so the next green overwrote it. Two failures four minutes apart left no recoverable explanation.

The wrapper now journals the detail for every nonzero exit, and a regression test holds that behaviour in place.

A signal is a state, not a history. If the only copy of a failure's cause lives in the slot that the next success rewrites, you have not lost an alert; you have lost the diagnosis. Keep the reason in a place whose lifetime is longer than the next poll.

Wrong time: a clock reading without a date

A nightly rhythm summary printed only times of day for three events, inside a file rewritten roughly every eleven minutes and carrying no staleness warning. Read on its own, it looks like last night. Recomputing from retained signatures showed all three components came from a night ten days earlier, while later nights had gaps that broke the sequence. The display was accurate down to the minute and wrong by a week and a half.

The summary now carries an absolute date for the event it describes. The line renders the date and the age — for example, "on 2026-11-10 (10d ago, not last night)" — and says "today" when it is current. A missing or malformed date makes no new claim at all, so a gap in the producer stays visible as a gap instead of being papered over by an old sentence. The header that once promised "one night of data" now says "all retained days". Eight tests were added; the scoped suite stayed green.

"A time of day" is not a timestamp. Without a date, every reader supplies the missing part from the most recent context, which is usually the present.

The shape underneath

The four repairs have one form. A check result is a statement whose truth depends on things outside the result: the bytes it ran, the instance it wrote, the record that keeps its cause, the day it describes. Each gap was a place where one of those dependencies was implicit and therefore unenforced. Each fix made it explicit and cheap to verify — generate the unit, read the marker, journal every failure, carry the date.

This is the continuation of the dark-lane work, not a separate topic. A dark lane asks whether the observer is alive. These four ask what the living observer is actually attached to. Both are questions about the observer, and neither can be answered by looking harder at the number it prints.

The durable part is the detector, not the patch. Each lane keeps the check that would catch a recurrence — a generated-unit assertion, a refused-foreign-write report, a test on the wrapper's journal, a dated summary — so the next ambiguity becomes a visible failure instead of a quiet, truthful answer to the wrong question.

Portworx Lets a Storage Pool Move Off a Failing Node
description:
TL;DR

  • Portworx Kube Datastore is a storage feature in Portworx Enterprise that lets a Kubernetes storage pool move from one node to another and maintains access to the volumes it contains.
  • The feature reached general availability in Portworx Enterprise 3.7.2, announced in a Portworx post on 9 November 2026, with Operator 26.5.0 and Stork 26.5.0 as the matching companion releases.
  • The design target is the replica tax created by writing several software copies of every volume on an already redundant SAN appliance: KDS lets a dynamic pool hold replica-1 volumes and move the pool itself when a node fails.
  • Portworx measured a live migration of a running CentOS Stream 9 virtual machine at under 10 seconds with zero observed I/O interruption, and recovery after a hard power-off at about 51 seconds, on a six-node OpenShift cluster backed by a Pure Storage FlashArray.
  • The GA release raises the per-node ceiling to 12 dynamic pools, adds compute-aware placement through WaitForFirstConsumer, supports local and remote FastPath on dynamic pools, and moves eligible pools off a node before a Portworx upgrade restarts it.
  • The requirements are narrow and stated: Red Hat OpenShift with a Pure FlashArray as the shared backend, replica-1 volumes in every dynamic pool, and an opt-in flag in the StorageCluster spec.

Portworx's diagram of the base model: a node with attached storage carries one or more pools, and a pool groups disks of the same class and type. Source: portworx.com/blog/portworx-kube-datastore-kds-introduction, retrieved 16 November 2026.

Storage pools follow the disks that sit under them

Portworx Enterprise organises storage into pools, and a pool is a logical grouping of disks of the same class and type. A Kubernetes node with attached storage carries one or more of them, depending on how many kinds of disk are attached. Replication happens between pools, and the replication factor is configurable.

That model works because local disks cannot travel. If a node dies, the storage attached to it dies with it, so the answer is a second copy on another node's pool. Portworx describes this as the correct architecture for local disks, and the post spends its first half explaining why the same answer produces a different result on a shared array.

The replica tax lands on an array that is already redundant

A Pure FlashArray is redundant on its own. When a Portworx cluster sits on one, the extra software copies of each volume still get written to the array. On a FlashArray those copies take no additional space, thanks to data reduction, and they do add work: more writes on the array, and more latency while the write waits for acknowledgement.

Portworx's diagram of the static model: a volume is replicated between pools, so losing one node still leaves a copy on another. Source: portworx.com/blog/portworx-kube-datastore-kds-introduction, retrieved 16 November 2026.

The tradeoff is the one an infrastructure team argues about every time it puts stateful workloads on shared storage. Storage-layer replication provides mobility and preserves data access after a node loss. On an already redundant array, array-level replication provides durability; repeated software copies add writes and acknowledgement latency. KDS answers that question for virtual machines, which is where the write cost lands hardest.

A dynamic pool holds replica-1 volumes and moves as a unit

Kube Datastore lets a pool move between Kubernetes nodes in three situations: a node failure is detected, an administrator moves the pool non-disruptively, or the system detects an imbalance. When a failure is detected, the pool migrates to another node and the virtual machine restarts there. During maintenance, the same move happens without disruption.

Portworx's diagram of the dynamic model: the pool carries replica-1 volumes and moves between nodes, and the array keeps the redundancy. Source: portworx.com/blog/portworx-kube-datastore-kds-introduction, retrieved 16 November 2026.

The mechanics rest on two properties. Dynamic pools use ReadWriteMany access modes and block-level intelligence, which lets both the source and the destination node hold access to a volume during a handoff. And because Portworx sits in the I/O path, it can redirect traffic for a virtual machine that is no longer local to its pool. Portworx sums the result as the efficiency of a single-replica volume with the resilience of a multi-replica system, borrowed from the high availability of the SAN underneath.

Live migration moved a running VM in under ten seconds

Portworx tested the behaviour on a six-node OpenShift cluster running the 3.6.0 Directed Availability build, backed by a Pure Storage FlashArray over iSCSI, with workloads on the px-csi-vm StorageClass at repl=1. The first test moved a running CentOS Stream 9 virtual machine from one worker node to another.

Portworx's timeline of the live migration test: the virtual machine moves between worker nodes while it keeps running. Source: portworx.com/blog/portworx-kube-datastore-kds-introduction, retrieved 16 November 2026.

The reported numbers are a migration duration under 10 seconds, zero observed I/O interruption, and a virtual machine that stayed running throughout. The post attributes that to the concurrent access the RWX and block configuration allows: the destination pre-attaches and shares the volume path during the transition, which removes the detach and reattach step that usually interrupts a containerised VM move.

A hard power-off came back in about 51 seconds

The second test removed the graceful part. Portworx performed a hard power-off on the worker node hosting a critical virtual machine, which forces the cluster to re-orchestrate the storage pool, work that goes beyond restarting a pod. Total recovery time was about 51 seconds.

The mechanism Portworx describes is a fastpath failover. When the new node tries to claim the volume while the old coordinator is still listed as active in the control plane, KDS registers a dual-attach and forces the volume to the new coordinator. The virtual machine comes back online in under a minute, and the pool converges on its new home.

Both figures describe a virtual machine. KDS supports containers, as the post states directly, and every published measurement comes from a KubeVirt environment; no published vendor measurement covers container workloads.

The GA release adds scale, placement and upgrade behaviour

Version 3.7.2 turns KDS from a Directed Availability feature into a supported one and adds several operational pieces. The per-node ceiling rises to 12 dynamic pools, up from 4 in the DA release, with headroom for four more so a node can absorb pools during maintenance or an outage. Per-cluster scale is stated at 5,000 volumes and 10,000 snapshots.

Placement changes with WaitForFirstConsumer binding. With WaitForFirstConsumer binding, the virtual machine is placed before the volume is provisioned, so data and workload start on the same node and traffic stays north-south to the SAN. Greenfield 3.7.2 installations get a replica-1 plus WaitForFirstConsumer storage class as the default.

Portworx's timeline of the failure test: the pool is prepared on another node as soon as the loss is detected, and the virtual machine restarts there. Source: portworx.com/blog/portworx-kube-datastore-kds-introduction, retrieved 16 November 2026.

On the data path, local and remote FastPath now both work on dynamic pools. Remote FastPath exports replicas over NVMe or TCP to the node running the virtual machine, with automatic promotion and demotion. Affinity groups keep related pools on one node and pull them back together after a failover, which limits how much a rebalance moves running virtual machines around.

Upgrades get their own change. Version 3.7.2 adds non-disruptive Portworx upgrades. The operator moves eligible pools off the node before restarting it, so virtual machines keep running through the upgrade.

What KDS requires before it will run

The platform requirement is the one that decides most deployments: KDS GA is supported on Red Hat OpenShift with a Pure FlashArray as the shared SAN backend. A dynamic pool contains replica-1 volumes only, so the array carries the redundancy and the cluster cannot mix replica counts inside a pool. Activation is opt-in, through spec.kubedatastore.enableDynamicPools: true in the StorageCluster.

Page capture of the post: "Introduction to Portworx KDS: Static to Dynamic Mobility", published 9 November 2026 by Chris Crow, Senior Technical Marketing Manager, Portworx. Source: portworx.com/blog/portworx-kube-datastore-kds-introduction, captured 16 November 2026.

Teams already running static pools have a conversion path. The pxvm tool converts legacy static pools to dynamic pools in place, in three steps: pxvm collect, pxvm migrate plan, then pxvm migrate apply --execute. The tool runs read-only until the apply step, and refuses to start unless the cluster is healthy, on 3.7.2 and has dynamic pools enabled.

Migration from VMware ties into the same placement change. Forklift and MTV migrations can use WaitForFirstConsumer storage classes, so virtual machines land hyperconverged on Portworx, and FlashArray XCopy offload lets large virtual machines around 10 TB migrate in hours.

What the measurements still leave open

The 51-second figure and the 10-second migration come from one test cluster with one array, described down to the storage class, and they say nothing about a cluster with slower array links or a heavier virtual machine. The post publishes no failure rate, no measurement on containers, and no comparison against a replicated pool under the same workload, so the replica tax argument rests on the architecture of writing fewer copies and on the write latency it removes.

Netics visual, 16 November 2026: the gains a dynamic pool brings and the four conditions Portworx attaches to them.

What a platform team can take from the post is the shape of the decision. A shared SAN with its own redundancy makes software replicas a cost that buys mobility, and KDS moves that cost into the pool: the pool becomes the unit that travels, and the array keeps the copy. Teams that plan their own sovereign infrastructure and cloud exit work meet the same decision from the other side: how long a workload stays unavailable when a node disappears without warning, and whether anyone learns the answer before a customer does.

Originally published on the Netics blog.

title: When Real Terrain Arrives: Failure Modes in Site Models Built on TopoExport Data, and How GenAnywhere, CityWeft, Meshy and CityEngine Contain Them
description:
There is a specific moment in every site project when the model stops being a proposal. It is not the first render, and it is not the client approval. It is the moment real elevation data arrives and gets imported into the file.

Everything before that moment is a design conversation. Everything after it is a reconciliation. I have watched that moment go well and go badly, and the difference is rarely talent. It is whether the team had a plan for the six failure modes that show up when real ground enters a model built on TopoExport data, and whether the rest of the stack, GenAnywhere for terrain, CityWeft for district layers, Meshy for generated objects, and CityEngine for procedural context, was arranged to contain them.

This is a catalogue of those failures. They are boring, they are common, and every one of them has a containment strategy.

What TopoExport Actually Delivers

TopoExport exports real terrain, contours and elevation, as usable three-dimensional geometry in the formats a site team already runs. That last part matters more than it sounds. The output is not a picture of a hill. It is a surface with coordinates, and coordinates are a contract.

A contract has terms. Which unit. Which datum. Which area of coverage. Which resolution. Which version of the source data. Most teams check none of these before importing, because the surface loads and looks right, and looking right is a very persuasive form of wrong.

Failure One: Unit and Scale Drift

The most expensive error in site modeling is also the least dramatic. A file exported in meters is imported as feet, or the reverse, and the resulting model is off by a factor of roughly 3.28 in every horizontal and vertical dimension.

What makes this failure dangerous is its plausibility. A site that is actually four hundred feet across becomes one hundred and twenty-two feet across, which still looks like a site. The slope becomes three times steeper, which still looks like a slope. Nothing in the viewport complains. The error only announces itself when a road alignment fails a design speed check or a drainage calculation returns a flow rate for a watershed that does not exist.

Containment is procedural, not technical. Import once, measure a known distance in both the source and the model, and write the scale factor into the project record. If the check is not written down, it will be repeated by the next person who opens the file.

Failure Two: Datum Mismatch

Vertical datum is the failure that survives the longest. One dataset is referenced to a local project datum, another to a national vertical reference, and a third to whatever the surveyor's software defaulted to in 1998. Import them all and the ground gains invisible steps that look like terrain and behave like terrain, which means nobody investigates them until construction.

The symptom is a site where the flood elevation, the building pad, and the stormwater outfall each seem reasonable individually but cannot all be true together. The fix is to establish one datum before the first import and refuse every file that cannot be reconciled to it. This is an administrative control. There is no software feature that makes a team care about datum.

Failure Three: Interpolation Cliffs

Contour data is sparse by nature. When a surface is generated from contours, the tool interpolates between them, and interpolation is where engineering reality gets smoothed into fiction.

The classic case is a retaining wall. The source contours step abruptly. The interpolated surface turns that step into a smooth ramp thirty feet wide, and a design that assumes a wall becomes a design that assumes a slope. Similar failures appear at curb lines, drainage channels, and loading docks, where the vertical difference is small in absolute terms and enormous in design consequence.

The containment strategy is visibility. Keep the source contours displayed alongside the interpolated mesh, and inspect every place where the design does real work: building edges, utility corridors, and the path water will take. If the mesh is smooth where the source is stepped, the mesh is lying and the contours are telling the truth.

Failure Four: Mesh Hygiene

Imported terrain is not clean geometry. It is a surface that has been through a conversion pipeline, and conversion pipelines produce duplicated vertices, coincident triangles, edges that do not meet, inverted normals, and occasional non-manifold junk where two surfaces were stitched badly.

None of this is visible. All of it is consequential. Boolean operations fail. Volume calculations return values that are close enough to be believed and wrong enough to matter. Clipping a section through a bad region produces a hole, and the hole gets modeled over instead of investigated.

Hygiene is the least glamorous containment strategy and the one that pays first. Run a mesh integrity check on import, weld duplicate vertices within a tolerance, remove degenerate triangles, and confirm that normals point up. Ten minutes of this prevents a week of downstream confusion, and it produces a record that reviewers can actually check.

Failure Five: Coverage Gaps at the Boundary

TopoExport delivers the area that was requested. Projects rarely stay inside that area.

The access road leaves the site. The drainage outfall crosses a property line. The view corridor extends three blocks. Each of those is a place where the model has real terrain and then abruptly does not, and the boundary of the import is usually a straight line that cuts across something meaningful.

The symptom is a model that behaves perfectly inside a rectangle and falls apart at its edge, which is exactly where interfaces are tested. Containment means mapping the coverage boundary before design begins and treating everything outside it as an explicit unknown rather than a default flat plane.

Failure Six: Provenance Loss After Editing

TopoExport makes the surface real. GenAnywhere then makes it arguable, and that is where provenance is most likely to disappear.

GenAnywhere is built for interactive terrain work: raising, cutting, and terracing while the mesh stays coherent. That is precisely the capability a design team needs once the survey is in, because a real site almost always needs a pad, a basin, or a terrace that the existing ground does not provide. The failure is not in the editing. It is in the handoff.

An edited surface that no longer knows which regions are surveyed and which are designed is a liability. Downstream teams will treat the whole thing as ground truth, and a cost estimate will be built on a grade that exists only in a proposal. The containment is a separation layer: keep the imported surface intact and immutable, keep design edits in a versioned overlay, and version every change with the reason it was made.

How the Rest of the Stack Contains the Rest

The four other tools in this stack are not interchangeable with TopoExport, and that is what makes them useful as containment.

GenAnywhere contains proposal risk. It lets a team argue about grade without overwriting the survey, as long as the edit history is kept separate and versioned.

CityWeft contains coordination risk. District layers are exported as separate, diffable documents with explicit boundaries, which means a change to the terrain assumption shows up as a visible difference rather than a silent shift in a merged file.

Meshy contains representation risk, on one condition. Generated objects are saved as artifacts, tagged as generated, and kept out of quantities and permit documents. A generated tank that looks correct and has no specification is a rendering, not an asset.

CityEngine contains context risk. Procedural massing beyond the site is generated from written rules, so when the terrain changes, the surrounding city can be regenerated rather than hand-fixed. The rules are the containment, and rules that are not versioned are not containment.

The Checklist That Prevents the Catalogue

None of these failures requires new software. They require a short, boring, repeatable check at the one moment that matters:

  1. Confirm unit and scale against a known distance.
  2. Reconcile every dataset to one vertical datum.
  3. Inspect interpolation at every place the design does real work.
  4. Run a mesh integrity check and weld duplicates.
  5. Map the coverage boundary and mark the outside as unknown.
  6. Separate surveyed ground from designed ground, and version the difference.

Real terrain is the best thing that can happen to a site model. It is also the moment the model acquires obligations. Teams that treat the import as a contract rather than a step get a surface they can build from. Teams that treat it as a background get a very convincing picture of a site that does not exist.

Python이 설치되어 있고 로컬 LLM 서버가 HTTP API를 제공한다고 가정합니다. 예를 들어 Ollama나 llama.cpp server처럼 OpenAI 호환 API를 제공하는 서버를 사용할 수 있으며, 실제 서버에 따라 주소와 모델 지정 방식을 바꿔야 합니다. PDF 파일은 docs 폴더에 준비하며, 스캔 이미지 PDF는 별도 OCR(이미지에서 문자를 읽는 기술)이 필요하고 OCR 결과도 원문과 대조해 품질을 확인해야 합니다.

구조는 PDF 텍스트 추출 → 청킹 → 임베딩 생성 → 벡터 저장 → 유사도 검색 → 로컬 LLM 답변 생성 순서로 진행합니다. 임베딩은 문장을 숫자 벡터로 바꾸는 과정이고, RAG는 검색 결과를 LLM의 질문 문맥에 넣어 답변하게 하는 방식입니다.

이 예제는 텍스트를 추출할 수 있는 PDF, paraphrase-multilingual-MiniLM-L12-v2의 128토큰 한도, OpenAI 호환 API를 제공하는 로컬 LLM 서버를 기준으로 합니다.

PDF 추출부터 벡터 검색까지

먼저 PDF 페이지별 텍스트와 페이지 번호를 함께 저장합니다. 페이지 정보가 있어야 답변이 어긋날 때 원문 위치를 다시 확인할 수 있습니다.

pip install pypdf sentence-transformers faiss-cpu requests numpy

from pathlib import Path
from pypdf import PdfReader
from sentence_transformers import SentenceTransformer
import faiss, json, numpy as np

model = SentenceTransformer("sentence-transformers/paraphrase-multilingual-MiniLM-L12-v2")
MAX_TOKENS = 100  # 이 모델의 128토큰 입력 한도보다 여유를 둠
OVERLAP = 20

def token_chunks(text: str):
    ids = model.tokenizer.encode(text, add_special_tokens=False)
    step = MAX_TOKENS - OVERLAP
    for start in range(0, len(ids), step):
        part = ids[start:start + MAX_TOKENS]
        if part:
            decoded = model.tokenizer.decode(part, skip_special_tokens=True).strip()
            if decoded:
                yield decoded

chunks, meta = [], []
for pdf in Path("docs").glob("*.pdf"):
    for page_no, page in enumerate(PdfReader(str(pdf)).pages, 1):
        text = (page.extract_text() or "").strip()
        for part in token_chunks(text):
            chunks.append(part)
            meta.append({"file": pdf.name, "page": page_no})
vectors = model.encode(chunks, normalize_embeddings=True)
index = faiss.IndexFlatIP(vectors.shape[1])
index.add(np.asarray(vectors, dtype="float32"))
faiss.write_index(index, "documents.faiss")
Path("metadata.json").write_text(json.dumps({"chunks": chunks, "meta": meta}, ensure_ascii=False), encoding="utf-8")

텍스트 추출 결과가 모두 비어 있으면 chunks도 비어 임베딩·인덱스 생성 단계가 실패할 수 있습니다. 먼저 docs에 PDF가 있는지와 페이지별 추출 텍스트가 비어 있지 않은지 확인하고, 스캔 문서라면 OCR 결과를 검토한 뒤 다시 진행합니다. 검색 결과가 없을 때도 빈 근거를 답변 근거로 취급하지 않아야 합니다.

임베딩과 원문 메타데이터는 함께 관리해야 합니다. 이 예제는 paraphrase-multilingual-MiniLM-L12-v2 모델 설정에서 공식 문서로 확인한 최대 입력 길이 128토큰을 넘기지 않도록 100토큰 단위와 20토큰 겹침을 사용합니다. 실제 문서에서는 문단·제목·문장 경계도 함께 고려하고, 다른 임베딩 모델을 쓰면 그 모델의 토큰 한도에 맞춰 값을 다시 정해야 합니다. 검색 시 질문도 같은 임베딩 모델로 변환한 뒤, 내적 또는 코사인 유사도(벡터 방향의 가까움)를 계산해 상위 결과를 가져옵니다. 예제에서는 동일한 임베딩 모델로 문서와 질문을 변환하며, 실제 서비스에서는 검색 목적에 맞는 모델을 선택하고 모델이 query/document 전용 인코딩을 지원한다면 해당 방식을 사용하는 것이 좋습니다. IndexFlatIP는 단순하고 이해하기 쉽지만 문서 수가 많아지면 별도 벡터 데이터베이스를 검토할 수 있습니다.

question = "환불 조건은 무엇인가요?"
q = model.encode([question], normalize_embeddings=True).astype("float32")
scores, ids = index.search(q, 4)
context = "\n\n".join(
    f"[{meta[i]['file']} p.{meta[i]['page']}]\n{chunks[i]}"
    for i in ids[0]
    if i >= 0
)

로컬 LLM 연결과 선택 기준

검색된 context와 질문을 프롬프트에 넣어 로컬 LLM API로 전송합니다. 아래 예시의 주소는 OpenAI 호환 API를 제공하는 로컬 서버의 예시이며, 실제 사용하는 서버에 맞게 주소와 모델 지정 방식을 변경해야 합니다. messages는 대화 메시지 목록, role은 메시지 발신 유형, content는 전달할 프롬프트를 뜻하고, model은 서버에 등록된 모델 이름입니다. 로컬 LLM 자체는 모델 크기, 양자화 방식, 서버 종류를 실행 환경과 요구 사항에 맞춰 선택해야 합니다. 프롬프트에는 “제공된 문서에 근거해 답하고, 근거가 없으면 모른다고 말하라”는 제한을 포함해야 합니다.

import requests

prompt = f"문서 근거만 사용해 답하세요. 근거가 없으면 모른다고 하세요.\n문서:\n{context}\n질문: {question}"
LOCAL_LLM_URL = "http://127.0.0.1:8000/v1/chat/completions"
LOCAL_LLM_MODEL = "YOUR_SERVER_MODEL_NAME"  # 서버에 실제 등록된 모델명으로 교체
response = requests.post(
    LOCAL_LLM_URL,
    json={
        "model": LOCAL_LLM_MODEL,
        "messages": [{"role": "user", "content": prompt}],
    },
    timeout=120,
)
print(response.json())
비교 항목 단순 파일 검색 RAG 파이프라인
검색 방식 키워드 일치 의미 유사도
답변 생성 직접 읽기 로컬 LLM 연결
구축 난이도 낮음 중간
적합한 문서 짧고 명확한 문서 여러 PDF와 자연어 질문

정확한 단어를 찾아야 하면 키워드 검색이 유리하고, 표현이 달라도 의미를 찾아야 하면 벡터 검색이 적합합니다. 문서 수가 적으면 파일 기반 저장으로 시작하고, 문서가 늘거나 필터링·권한 관리가 필요하면 벡터 데이터베이스를 선택하세요.

자주 묻는 질문

스캔 PDF도 바로 검색할 수 있나요?

아닙니다. 텍스트 추출 결과가 비어 있으면 OCR로 페이지 이미지를 문자로 변환한 뒤 같은 청킹 과정을 적용해야 합니다. 표와 각주가 많은 문서는 추출 후 원문과 내용이 맞는지 일부 페이지를 확인하세요.

RAG를 쓰면 환각이 완전히 사라지나요?

아닙니다. 검색 결과가 틀리거나 관련 청크가 누락되면 로컬 LLM도 잘못 답할 수 있습니다. 답변에 페이지 메타데이터를 표시하고, 중요한 내용은 원문과 대조하는 절차를 두는 것이 좋습니다.

결론

PDF RAG는 추출 품질, 청크 설계, 임베딩 일관성, 검색 결과 검증이 핵심입니다. 작은 문서로 파이프라인을 검증한 뒤 규모와 보안 요구에 맞춰 저장소를 확장하세요.

관련 글

  • LM Studio로 로컬 LLM 처음 써보기 (GUI 중심)
  • RAG(Retrieval-Augmented Generation), AI 언어 모델의 지평을 넓히다
  • 로컬 LLM 구축하기: Ollama 설치부터 모델 실행까지

이 글의 원문은 내 PDF 문서를 로컬 LLM에게 검색시키기 — RAG 실전 구축 에 있습니다. (Originally published on Briefold)

title: Claude account disabled? Preserve the evidence before you appeal
description:
You open Claude and see a disabled-account notice. Before changing settings or trying a collection of fixes, save what the screen actually says. A short, accurate incident record is easier to review than a long explanation built around a guessed cause.

I checked the official appeal guidance and put together the preparation workflow below. The evidence layout is an editorial suggestion, not a list of mandatory appeal-form fields.

Preserve the notice before changing anything

Save the full notice privately. Record the product surface, the time, and the time zone. Keep enough context to tell whether the message concerns your account, an organization, or a specific operation. A cropped image containing only the word “disabled” leaves that distinction out.

Keep the original file unchanged. Create a separate redacted copy for submission, removing unrelated personal information and project content. If you received a notification, preserve that original too. Do not replace its wording with your interpretation.

A terminal error belongs in the record as an error. Unless the notice actually says the account is disabled, do not silently turn it into a suspension claim.

Build a timeline that separates observation from inference

Write down the last known successful use, the first appearance of the notice, what you were doing immediately beforehand, and any steps you have already tried. Approximate times should be marked as approximate. An unknown field is more useful than an invented timestamp.

A compact worksheet can use these columns:

Time and zone Surface Action taken Exact message Attachment
Fill from your records Name the page or tool Describe the action Preserve the wording Use a local filename

Keep observations and theories separate. “The notice appeared after this action” records a sequence. “This action caused the suspension” adds a causal claim that the sequence alone cannot establish.

If a log is relevant, extract the smallest useful portion. Review it for API keys, session tokens, private conversations, and unrelated identifiers before sharing it. An incident report should not become a second way to lose control of your account.

Keep environment diagnostics separate from the appeal

An environment report can describe an observation; it cannot decide why an account was disabled. Preserve the original notice before running diagnostics or changing network settings. Changing several things at once also makes your timeline harder to interpret.

If you use a diagnostic script, read its source and documentation first. Understand what it reads, which destinations it contacts, and where output is saved. If those details are unavailable, skip that step. You can still prepare the notice and timeline without a script.

Use the official appeal route

Anthropic's Safeguards warnings and appeals guidance directs users who believe their account was wrongly suspended to sign in with the affected account and use the linked appeal form. Access to that form requires being signed in.

Follow the fields on the actual form. Describe the restriction you observed, when it appeared, the actions your records support, and what you want reviewed. Keep guesses about the cause clearly separate. Save the submission confirmation so any later additions can refer back to the same record.

Affiliate disclosure

The following are affiliate links, and I may earn a commission from purchases through them. They are commercial references, not steps in the appeal workflow. Buying a third-party tool does not constitute an appeal and provides no basis for claiming an account will be restored. Do not use these services to evade an account restriction.
