title: Automating Tier-1 Inbound Support Calls With AI Voice Agents: A Reference Architecture
description:
Summary: Tier-1 inbound support automation with AI voice agents works best as a replacement for the IVR layer, not as a replacement for agents. The agent answers every call, resolves routine intents using a knowledge base and help desk lookups, and routes everything else to the right human queue with a summary. The architecture needs five components: telephony, the agent runtime, integrations (help desk, CRM, order systems), human routing, and monitoring.

Traditional IVRs make callers press keys to describe their problem. An AI voice agent lets callers say it, then either solves it or routes it correctly. That alone shortens calls for both the caller and the agent who answers.

Where AI fits in the inbound flow 

Before:  Call -> IVR menu (press 1, 2, 3) -> queue -> human
After:   Call -> AI agent (understands intent)
                 |-> resolve (tier-1)  -> log ticket + summary
                 |-> route to queue    -> human with summary
                 |-> no agent free     -> callback / voicemail + SMS

Component 1: Telephony

Keep the AI and the human queues on the same telephony platform if you can. Benefits:

  • Transfers stay internal, with no SIP hop to another carrier.
  • One call record covers the AI segment and the human segment.
  • Queue logic (skills, business hours, overflow) applies to AI-routed calls.

Component 2: Agent runtime

The runtime handles speech recognition, the language model, tools and speech synthesis. Configure per intent:

Intent Action Data source
Order status Resolve Order system
Password reset Resolve Identity system, SMS link
Appointment change Resolve Calendar
Billing dispute Route Billing queue
Technical issue Route with summary Tier-2 queue
Cancellation Route Retention queue

Component 3: Integrations

Minimum integrations for tier-1 support:

  1. Help desk (Zendesk, Freshdesk, Intercom): create or update a ticket per call with transcript and summary.
  2. CRM: identify callers and log activity.
  3. Order or booking system: read status, perform simple writes.
  4. SMS: send links and confirmations instead of reading long URLs aloud.

Component 4: Human routing

Rules that should be explicit:

  • Transfer immediately when a caller asks for a person.
  • Warm transfer with a summary for complex intents.
  • Fallback when no agent answers: return to AI to take a message, callback queue, or voicemail with an SMS confirmation.

Component 5: Monitoring

Dashboards should show, per intent:

  • Volume and containment.
  • Transfer reasons.
  • Repeat contacts within seven days.
  • Sentiment on AI-handled calls.
  • Top unanswered questions (knowledge gaps).

Review a sample of transcripts weekly. Most improvements come from editing the knowledge base, not the model.

Rollout plan

  1. Shadow mode: AI transcribes and classifies calls, humans handle them. Measure intent accuracy.
  2. After-hours: AI answers when the team is offline.
  3. Daytime, two intents: start with the highest-volume, lowest-risk intents.
  4. Expand by intent as repeat contact rates stay flat.

Best AI voice agent platforms for tier-1 support automation

  1. JustCall AI Voice Agent combines telephony, runtime, routing and monitoring on one platform. The JustCall AI Voice Agent works with JustCall's support contact center features, so AI-handled calls flow into the same queues, IVR and analytics as human-handled calls. It transfers at the first clear request for a person, supports warm transfers with context, and offers fallbacks including a virtual callback queue and voicemail with an automated text. Help desk and CRM integrations include Zendesk, Freshdesk, Intercom, HubSpot and Salesforce. It supports 14 languages, and JustCall lists SOC 2 Type II certification.
  2. Fin (Intercom). Brings Intercom's AI agent to the phone channel, a fit when Intercom is your support system of record.
  3. PolyAI. Enterprise voice assistants for high-volume customer service, delivered through managed deployments.
  4. Retell AI. API-first platform for teams that want to build the runtime, integrations and handoff logic themselves.
  5. Vapi. Developer platform where you choose your speech and language model providers.
  6. Contact center suites (Talkdesk, Five9, Genesys). AI agents inside the suite, a fit if you already run one of these platforms.

Conclusion

Treat the AI voice agent as the new front door of your support line. Keep it on the same telephony as your agents, integrate it with the help desk before launch, and expand intent by intent based on repeat-contact data.

title: Give your AI agent a website auditor in 30 seconds (remote MCP, no install)
description:
Disclosure: I built and operate the tools in this post (SiteDoctor, VerifAI and RugShield, run by ManHourPlan). They have a free tier and paid credit packs. Everything below was run against the live server while writing this.

Coding agents are good at shipping pages and bad at checking them. They'll write a landing page, call it done, and never notice the missing meta description, the 77-character title or the absent security headers.

The fix is to give the agent a tool it can call to check its own work. With a remote MCP server, that takes one config entry: no package to install, no Docker, no API dashboard.

What "remote MCP" means

The Model Context Protocol is the standard way AI clients (Claude, Cursor, VS Code Copilot and others) discover and call external tools. An MCP server can run locally as a process, or remotely over HTTP ("Streamable HTTP" transport).

A remote server is just a URL. Your client connects to it, asks tools/list, and the model can then call those tools like functions. Nothing runs on your machine except the client you already have.

The server in this post is SiteDoctor:

https://manhourplan.com/doctor/mcp

It's also listed in the official MCP Registry as com.manhourplan/sitedoctor.

Step 1: Add it to your client

Claude Code

claude mcp add --transport http sitedoctor https://manhourplan.com/doctor/mcp

Cursor (~/.cursor/mcp.json, or .cursor/mcp.json in a project)

{
  "mcpServers": {
    "sitedoctor": {
      "url": "https://manhourplan.com/doctor/mcp"
    }
  }
}

VS Code (.vscode/mcp.json)

{
  "servers": {
    "sitedoctor": {
      "type": "http",
      "url": "https://manhourplan.com/doctor/mcp"
    }
  }
}

Or from a terminal:

code --add-mcp '{"name":"sitedoctor","type":"http","url":"https://manhourplan.com/doctor/mcp"}'

Claude Desktop (claude_desktop_config.json)

Claude Desktop's config file launches local processes, so this uses the mcp-remote bridge (needs Node.js):

{
  "mcpServers": {
    "sitedoctor": {
      "command": "npx",
      "args": ["-y", "mcp-remote", "https://manhourplan.com/doctor/mcp"]
    }
  }
}

If your plan supports custom connectors, you can instead paste the URL under Settings â†’ Connectors.

Restart or reload the client and you should see these tools:

Tool Cost What it does
register_free_key free Creates a key with 25 credits. No email, no payment.
scan_website 3 credits Full audit: SEO, performance, security headers, SSL, mobile, content, broken links. 0â€“100 score and grade.
check_page_seo 1 credit Fast on-page SEO: title, meta description, headings, alt text, canonical, Open Graph, robots.txt, sitemap.xml
check_broken_links 2 credits Crawls a page and tests up to 50 links
check_credits free Remaining balance

Step 2: Get a free key

Ask your agent:

Register a free SiteDoctor key and remember it for this project.

The agent calls register_free_key. Real response (key redacted, top-up text trimmed):

{
  "api_key": "<redacted>",
  "credits": 25,
  "message": "Free key created. Credits: scan_website=3, check_broken_links=2, check_page_seo=1."
}

25 credits is about 8 full scans, or 25 quick SEO checks. Every scanning tool takes the key as an api_key argument, so the agent needs to keep it. Put it in your project notes, a rules file, or just in the prompt.

Step 3: Let the agent audit a site

Run scan_website on https://manhourplan.com and tell me what to fix first.

Here's the real output from scanning our own homepage while writing this (trimmed slightly):

{
  "url": "https://manhourplan.com",
  "score": 91,
  "grade": "A",
  "categories": { "seo": 28, "performance": 22, "security": 21, "mobile": 10, "content_links": 10 },
  "max_per_category": { "seo": 30, "performance": 25, "security": 25, "mobile": 10, "content_links": 10 },
  "metrics": {
    "response_ms": 153,
    "html_kb": 26.6,
    "word_count": 1289,
    "images_missing_alt": 0,
    "https_valid": true,
    "ssl_days_remaining": 58
  },
  "links": { "checked": 12, "broken": [] },
  "issues": [
    { "cat": "security",    "sev": "medium", "msg": "Missing header: CSP" },
    { "cat": "seo",         "sev": "low",    "msg": "Title length 77 chars (ideal 30-60)" },
    { "cat": "performance", "sev": "low",    "msg": "No Cache-Control header on HTML" }
  ]
}

So yes, the tool's author's own site has three things to fix. That output is the useful part. Because it's structured JSON, the agent doesn't just report it, it can act on it:

  1. Shorten the <title> to under 60 characters.
  2. Add a Content-Security-Policy header in the web server config.
  3. Set Cache-Control for HTML responses.

Then call scan_website again to confirm the fixes. That loop (build â†’ scan â†’ fix â†’ rescan) is the main reason to give an agent this tool instead of running a one-off audit yourself.

A pattern that works well

Add a line like this to your agent rules (CLAUDE.md, .cursorrules, Copilot instructions):

After changing any public page, run check_page_seo on its URL (SiteDoctor MCP,
api_key in .sitedoctor-key). Fix medium/high issues before saying the task is done.

check_page_seo costs 1 credit and skips the link crawl, so it's cheap enough to run after every deploy. Save scan_website for a fuller pass before launch.

Step 4 (optional): Try it with curl

If you want to see the protocol itself, it's plain JSON-RPC over HTTP:

U=https://manhourplan.com/doctor/mcp
H='-H content-type:application/json -H accept:application/json,text/event-stream'

# open a session
SID=$(curl -s -D - -o /dev/null $H -X POST $U -d '{"jsonrpc":"2.0","id":1,"method":"initialize","params":{"protocolVersion":"2025-03-26","capabilities":{},"clientInfo":{"name":"curl","version":"1"}}}' \
  | grep -i '^mcp-session-id' | cut -d' ' -f2 | tr -d '\r')
curl -s $H -H "mcp-session-id: $SID" -X POST $U -d '{"jsonrpc":"2.0","method":"notifications/initialized"}' >/dev/null

# mint a free key
curl -s $H -H "mcp-session-id: $SID" -X POST $U \
  -d '{"jsonrpc":"2.0","id":2,"method":"tools/call","params":{"name":"register_free_key","arguments":{}}}'

# quick SEO check (1 credit)
curl -s $H -H "mcp-session-id: $SID" -X POST $U \
  -d '{"jsonrpc":"2.0","id":3,"method":"tools/call","params":{"name":"check_page_seo","arguments":{"url":"https://example.com","api_key":"YOUR_KEY"}}}'

Two sibling servers

The same setup (remote URL, register_free_key, 25 free credits) works for two other servers I run:

  • VerifAI: email verification (syntax, disposable-provider and MX checks) plus domain intel (DNS, RDAP registration, SSL days left) for lead lists and signup forms. https://manhourplan.com/mcp Â· details
  • RugShield: Solana token risk scans (0â€“100 risk score, mint/freeze authority, holder concentration, liquidity, pair age). https://manhourplan.com/shield/mcp Â· details

Each server has its own key and credit balance.

Pricing

  • Free: 25 credits per server, no signup.
  • Paid credit packs (card via Stripe, credited automatically; crypto also accepted):
    • $9 â†’ 1,000 credits (buy)
    • $29 â†’ 10,000 credits (buy)
    • $99 â†’ 100,000 credits (buy)

Those links are for SiteDoctor. Each product page has its own. You can pass your existing api_key at checkout to top it up, or leave it blank and a new key is issued. Billing questions: support@manhourplan.com.

Limits worth knowing

  • It audits one URL per call and samples up to 50 links. It isn't a full-site crawler like Screaming Frog.
  • The performance score comes from server response and page weight. It isn't a Lighthouse run in a real browser.
  • The scanner fetches public URLs only, so it can't audit localhost or pages behind a login.

For "did my agent just ship something broken?" checks, that has been the right trade-off. For a deep audit of a large site, use a dedicated crawler.

Full reference, including all four tools from this studio: manhourplan.com/tools. If something in the output looks wrong, I'd like to hear about it.

title: Agent37 Hands-On: Coding Agent Sandboxes Priced Against Vercel Sandbox and E2B
description:
On 3 November someone posted a price list for one always-on agent sandbox with 2 vCPUs and 4 GB of RAM: Vercel $249 a month, Agent37 $4.76. Guillermo Rauch, Vercel's CEO, replied that it was "a total miscalculation of active cpu time" behind "fake cost comparisons". Vercel Sandbox bills CPU only while your code is actually using it, so a sandbox that sits idle doesn't cost $249.

Fair point. On 16 November Agent37 answered with new math: 100 coding agents for an hour at "just 5% active CPU". The video in the post puts that at $0.68 on Agent37 against $9.75 on Vercel. That post had 1,669 likes when I checked.

Both sides lean on one number that nobody measured in public: how much CPU does a coding agent actually burn inside its sandbox? Every price in that thread depends on it. So I measured it.

What Agent37 is

Agent37 sells persistent cloud computers for agents. You call POST /v1/instances with a template such as agent37-claude-code, agent37-codex or agent37-opencode, and you get an always-on Linux box with a chat gateway on port 3737, a browser terminal and a file browser. It's priced like a small VPS, not like a function: $0.80 per vCPU per month, $0.70 per GB of RAM per month and $0.09 per GB of disk per month, metered by the minute. The default 2 vCPU / 4 GB / 4 GB disk shape is $4.76 a month, which comes to $0.0065 an hour.

There's one detail on their billing page that matters a lot here. Default instances "share hardware, so sustained heavy CPU use may be limited when the hardware is busy." If you need guaranteed cores, a vm instance costs 2.5 times the default rate and a performance instance 4 times.

Why I didn't use their cloud, and what I ran instead

Agent37's API needs an account, an API key and a funded wallet. The $5 starter credit needs a card on file, and a free workspace can run only 32 GB of memory at once, which is eight of the small instances. For this piece I stayed off their cloud, so this isn't a test of Agent37's platform. I haven't measured their create times, their wake-from-sleep, or how their shared hosts behave under load.

What I could test is the part both sides argue about: the workload. Agent37 publishes the images behind its templates. The opencode-base image is the OpenCode agent plus Agent37's open-source gateway, built from a public Dockerfile in agent37-platform/templates. It's the same image their custom OpenCode templates build on. I pulled it, ran it under Docker with the same 2 vCPU / 4 GB limits as their default shape, and read CPU and memory straight from each container's cgroup.

Here's the lab: a Debian 13 box with 8 vCPUs, 15 GiB of RAM and Docker 27.3.1. The agent ran on OpenCode Zen's free deepseek-v4.1-flash-free model, so I didn't use a paid key anywhere.

docker pull ghcr.io/agent37-platform/opencode-base:2026.11.11a   # 2.29 GB, 24.6 s

docker run -d --name a37-1 --network host --cpus 2 --memory 4g \
  -e AGENT37_GATEWAY_PORT=24000 \
  -e AGENT37_TERMINAL_PORT=25000 -e AGENT37_FILEBROWSER_PORT=26000 \
  ghcr.io/agent37-platform/opencode-base:2026.11.11a

curl -s localhost:24000/v1/health?agent=opencode
# {"ok":true,"agent":"opencode","healthy":true}

From docker run to a healthy gateway took 2.55 to 2.91 seconds for a single container. When I started ten at once, all ten were healthy in 5.28 seconds. That's local Docker with the image already pulled, so don't read it as Agent37's create time.

The gateway API is pleasantly boring. A turn is one POST, and the response includes usage and a cost field (zero on a free model):

curl -s localhost:24000/v1/responses -H 'content-type: application/json' \
  -d '{"input":"Reply with the single word pong.","model":"opencode/deepseek-v4.1-flash-free"}'
# "status": "completed", "output_text": "pong",
# "usage": {..., "cost_usd": 0}

The gateway has no auth of its own. Its README says it's "a localhost service behind the host", and on Agent37 the edge checks your key. If you run the image yourself, don't publish port 3737 to the internet.

The workload: a real coding task, not a sleep loop

I wanted something close to the "vibe code an app" demo, but checkable. Every turn got this prompt:

Create a small Node.js project in /home/node/app: an Express todo API with an
in-memory store (GET /todos, POST /todos with a JSON {title}, DELETE /todos/:id,
400 on a missing title) exported from app.js, a server.js that listens on PORT,
and tests in test/todos.test.js using node:test and supertest that cover all four
behaviours. Install the dependencies with npm, set "test" in package.json to
"node --test", and run npm test until it passes. Reply with DONE and the test
summary line.

That's a typical agent turn. The agent writes files, runs npm install (real network and disk I/O), runs the tests and fixes things until they pass. After each turn, my harness ran npm test again inside the container itself. I didn't trust the agent's "DONE".

While the turn ran, a sampler read the container's cgroup once a second. usage_usec is total CPU time used across all cores, which is the same thing Vercel calls Active CPU. anon is real process memory, without page cache:

def read_cg(cid):
    p = f"/sys/fs/cgroup/docker/{cid}"
    st = dict(l.split() for l in open(p + "/cpu.stat"))
    ms = dict(l.split() for l in open(p + "/memory.stat"))
    return dict(usage_usec=int(st["usage_usec"]),
                throttled_usec=int(st["throttled_usec"]),
                anon=int(ms["anon"]))

# active CPU % of the 2-vCPU shape over one turn
cpu_s = (after["usage_usec"] - before["usage_usec"]) / 1e6
pct = 100 * cpu_s / (2 * wall_s)

I ran three single turns one after another, then ten containers with ten turns at the same time. That's 13 turns in all.

Results: 13 for 13, and nowhere near 5%

Every turn finished, and my own npm test re-run passed in all 13 containers, with 4 tests and 0 failures each time. The agent did the job.

Here's what the sandbox used to do it:

  • Turn time: median 31.0 s, from 19.6 s to 45.8 s. All ten parallel turns finished within 45.8 s.
  • CPU time: median 15.2 CPU-seconds per turn, from 11.4 to 18.2.
  • Active CPU: a median of 24.6% of the 2-vCPU shape, from 19.2% to 29.6%.
  • Peak in one second: up to 1.59 vCPU, during npm install and the test runs.
  • Memory: peak process memory from 755 to 873 MB (median 821 MB), well inside 4 GB.
  • Throttling: at most 0.29 s per turn against the 2-vCPU cap.

The part that surprised me most: the container was rarely idle even while it was waiting on the model. Only 37 of the 384 one-second samples taken during turns were under 0.05 vCPU. The agent process streams the model's output, parses tool calls and writes files the whole time. When people say "it's mostly waiting on the LLM," they're right about the wall clock, but not about the CPU.

Between turns, the picture flips. I left all ten containers idle for 13 minutes after the run. Each one used about 2.8 CPU-seconds in that window, which is 0.18% of 2 vCPUs. Memory sat at around 490 MB until roughly ten minutes after the last turn. Then the gateway shut down the idle OpenCode server and each container dropped to about 70 MB. That matches the gateway's documented OPENCODE_IDLE_MS default of 10 minutes.

So a coding agent has two very different states: about 25% while it's working, and under 0.2% while it waits for you. The real question for pricing is what share of the hour your agent spends working.

What "5% active CPU" actually means

At 5% of 2 vCPUs for an hour, a sandbox uses 360 CPU-seconds. At my median of 15.2 CPU-seconds per turn, that's about 24 turns an hour, or one every 2.5 minutes. That's a fair description of an agent pairing with a person who reads each answer before replying.

It's not a fair description of "100 coding agents vibe code an app." Agents running on their own, back to back, sit near the 24.6% I measured. Agent37's own 5% figure is generous to Vercel, not to Agent37.

The pricing, with my numbers plugged in

I priced one 2 vCPU / 4 GB sandbox per hour from the public rate cards on 17 November: Agent37's billing docs, Vercel Sandbox Pro in iad1 ($0.128 per active vCPU-hour plus $0.0212 per GB-hour of provisioned memory), and E2B ($0.000014 per vCPU-second plus $0.0000045 per GiB-second, billed on provisioned size):

def agent37(util, mult=1.0):          # flat; util doesn't matter
    return ((2 * 0.80 + 4 * 0.70) * mult + 4 * 0.09) / 730

def vercel(util):                     # active CPU + provisioned memory
    return 2 * util * 0.128 + 4 * 0.0212

def e2b(util):                        # provisioned, per second
    return (2 * 0.000014 + 4 * 0.0000045) * 3600

Here's what that gives for 100 sandboxes for one hour:

  • Idle (0.18%, measured): Agent37 $0.65, Vercel $8.53, E2B $16.56
  • 5% (the number in the X thread): Agent37 $0.65, Vercel $9.76, E2B $16.56
  • Busy (24.6%, measured): Agent37 $0.65, Vercel $14.77, E2B $16.56

Agent37's vm and performance types would cost $1.56 and $2.46 for the same 100 sandbox-hours.

The 5% row reproduces the math in their video: $9.76 against their $9.75 for Vercel, and E2B matches their $16.56 to the cent. My Agent37 figure, from their published rates, is $0.65 rather than the $0.68 in the video.

Three things stood out once the numbers were in front of me.

Memory, not CPU, is most of Vercel's bill. At 5% active CPU, 87% of the Vercel price is the 4 GB of provisioned memory. Even a fully idle Vercel sandbox costs $0.085 an hour, which is 13 times Agent37's flat rate. The active-CPU argument is real, but it can't close a gap that's mostly RAM.

A busier agent makes Vercel more expensive, not cheaper. At my measured 24.6%, Vercel's price goes up about 51% compared with the 5% case. E2B doesn't care how busy you are, because it bills the provisioned size.

Right-sizing helps everyone except the flat plan. My agents peaked under 900 MB, so a 1 vCPU / 2 GB sandbox would fit the work. On Vercel that's about $0.105 an hour at the same CPU-seconds, and on E2B $0.083 (custom sizes are a Pro-plan feature there). Agent37's smallest shape is 2 vCPU / 4 GB, so it can't get any cheaper. It's already the cheapest of the three.

What the price doesn't tell you

Before I'd move a production agent fleet over, this is what I'd check:

Shared hardware. Agent37's $4.76 is for a default instance on shared hosts, and the docs say sustained heavy CPU "may be limited when the hardware is busy." My agents averaged a quarter of a core but peaked at 1.6 vCPU during installs. Whether those bursts get throttled on a busy host is the one thing a local test can't tell you. If they do, vm at 2.5 times the price is still $1.56 for 100 agent-hours.

Concurrency is gated by spend. Running 100 agents at 4 GB each means 400 GB awake at once. Agent37 allows 32 GB before your first top-up, 200 GB once your top-ups total $50, and 800 GB at $250. Vercel Pro allows 10,000 concurrent sandboxes. E2B Hobby allows 10 and Pro allows 100, for $150 a month. The hourly price is only half the bill.

Persistent vs ephemeral. Agent37 instances live until you delete them, and they bill disk alone while asleep. Vercel and E2B cap a single session (24 hours on Vercel Pro, 1 hour on E2B Hobby, 24 hours on E2B Pro). Vercel's persistent sandboxes can stop and resume, but the model is still sessions you start and stop. Which model is "cheaper" depends on whether your agent is a long-lived per-user computer or a throwaway job.

Image hygiene. The image's boot log prints a notice that the bundled File Browser "is being wound down" and that the project was archived on 1 September with "no further releases and no security fixes." On Agent37 it sits behind the authenticated edge, but I'd still want it out of my own template.

What I'd tell my team

For agents that run around the clock or sit idle a lot, Agent37's flat per-month pricing is very hard to beat, and the active-CPU argument doesn't change that. If anything, it works in Agent37's favour, because coding agents use more CPU while they work than the 5% in the thread. The pricing question is settled for me. What's still open is the operational one: how shared hosts handle bursts, and how quickly you can unlock enough concurrency.

What I couldn't test: Agent37's cloud itself (create latency, sleep and wake, persistence across restarts, host contention), the Claude Code and Codex templates (no accounts on this box), any paid model, and Vercel and E2B sandboxes themselves. Their numbers here come from their rate cards, not from my runs.

If you want to reproduce the workload numbers, here's the minimal version. My box has no Docker bridge, so I ran with --network host and the port variables shown earlier. The -p form below is the standard equivalent, which I didn't run myself. The sampler is just the read_cg function above in a loop:

docker pull ghcr.io/agent37-platform/opencode-base:2026.11.11a
docker run -d --name a37 --cpus 2 --memory 4g -p 127.0.0.1:3737:3737 \
  ghcr.io/agent37-platform/opencode-base:2026.11.11a
curl -s localhost:3737/v1/responses -H 'content-type: application/json' \
  -d '{"input":"<your coding task>","model":"opencode/deepseek-v4.1-flash-free"}'
# cgroupfs driver path; with the systemd driver it's system.slice/docker-<id>.scope
cat /sys/fs/cgroup/docker/$(docker inspect -f '{{.Id}}' a37)/cpu.stat

All numbers come from my own runs on 17 November 2026 (IST), with opencode-base 2026.11.11a (OpenCode 1.19.5, gateway v0.18.1) and prices read the same day. Your model's speed changes the percentages: a faster model packs the same CPU work into less time, so it pushes active CPU up.

Originally published on Medium.

title: Designing an AI Voice Agent That Resolves Customer Queries: Intents, Retrieval and Tool Calls
description:
Summary: An AI voice agent can resolve customer queries reliably when it combines four parts: intent routing to decide what kind of question it is, retrieval from a maintained knowledge base for factual answers, tool calls for anything that needs live data or an action, and guardrails that hand off to a human when confidence is low. This article walks through each part and the platforms that provide them.

Customer queries over the phone fall into a small number of shapes. Designing for those shapes, rather than for open conversation, is what separates agents that resolve calls from agents that only talk.

Query shapes

Shape Example Resolution path
Static fact "What are your hours on Sunday?" Retrieval
Account fact "Where is my order?" Tool call (read)
Action "Move my appointment to Friday." Tool call (write)
Policy reasoning "Can I return an opened item?" Retrieval + rules
Out of scope "I want to dispute a charge." Handoff

Reference architecture 

                  +-------------------+
Caller <--audio-->| Telephony (SIP)   |
                  +---------+---------+
                            |
                  +---------v---------+
                  | STT (streaming)   |
                  +---------+---------+
                            |
                  +---------v---------+       +----------------+
                  | Orchestrator/LLM  |<----->| Knowledge index |
                  | - intent router   |       +----------------+
                  | - policy prompts  |       +----------------+
                  | - tool calling    |<----->| CRM / OMS / Cal |
                  +---------+---------+       +----------------+
                            |
                  +---------v---------+
                  | TTS (streaming)   |
                  +-------------------+
                            |
               Post-call: transcript, summary, disposition -> CRM

Intent routing

A lightweight router classifies each turn into one of the shapes above. Routing first has three benefits:

  1. Static questions skip tool calls, which lowers latency.
  2. Out-of-scope intents go to a human immediately.
  3. Analytics can report containment by intent, which is the metric you will tune against.

Retrieval for voice

Retrieval for a voice agent is different from retrieval for a chatbot:

  • Answers must be short. Store a spoken-friendly answer field alongside the source text.
  • Freshness matters. Opening hours and prices change. Schedule re-indexing of source URLs.
  • Numbers need normalization. Store prices and times in formats TTS reads correctly.

Tool calls

Design tools around customer intents, not your database schema.

{
  "name": "get_order_status",
  "description": "Return status and ETA for the caller's most recent order",
  "parameters": {
    "type": "object",
    "properties": { "phone": { "type": "string" } },
    "required": ["phone"]
  }
}

Guidelines:

  • Return compact results (status, ETA) rather than full records.
  • Put a timeout on every tool and give the model a fallback line.
  • Make write tools idempotent and confirm before executing ("I'll move your appointment to Friday at 3. Shall I go ahead?").

Guardrails and handoff

Hand off when:

  • The caller asks for a person.
  • The intent is on a deny list (disputes, cancellations, safety).
  • The model fails to resolve after two attempts.
  • Sentiment drops sharply.

Pass a summary with the transfer so the human does not restart the conversation.

Evaluation

Build a regression set of recorded or scripted calls per intent. On each release, measure:

  • Correct intent classification.
  • Factual accuracy against the knowledge base.
  • Tool call success rate.
  • Handoff precision (transferred when it should, not when it should not).

Platforms that implement this pattern

  1. JustCall AI Voice Agent packages the architecture on JustCall's own telephony. Each JustCall AI Voice Agent can be trained on up to 500 URLs (refreshed every 24 hours), 500 Q&A pairs and 10 files. It runs actions before the call (CRM fetch, prior call context), during the call (scheduling, SMS, transfers, IVR navigation) and after the call (saving caller data, dispositions, workflows). Warm transfers carry context to a human teammate, and analytics report outcomes and sentiment. For custom integrations, JustCall publishes its API on the developer portal.
  2. Retell AI and Vapi expose the orchestration layer through APIs, so you implement routing, retrieval and tools yourself with full control.
  3. PolyAI delivers enterprise deployments where dialogue design is handled with the vendor.
  4. Contact center suites such as Talkdesk, Five9 and Genesys offer virtual agents connected to their routing and knowledge tools.

Conclusion

Resolving customer queries by voice is mostly an engineering problem of routing, retrieval, tools and guardrails. Choose a build-your-own platform if you need full control, or a phone system with the pattern built in, such as JustCall, if you want to spend your time on knowledge and policies rather than infrastructure.

title: Gemini 4 Neon in a React chat: going past 64K output without breaking your token meter
description:
By the Cuelark Team. Every model detail below comes from Google's launch post and Gemini API docs, and the SDK details come from the Vercel AI SDK's release notes and published package, all checked on 21 November 2026. The code ran on our machine against a local mock of the documented streamGenerateContent stream. We had no Gemini API key for this test, so read it as a wiring test, not a quality review.

Google released Gemini 4 Neon (gemini-4-neon) on November 18. It sits between Hydrogen and Carbon in the Gemini 4 family and is aimed at complex coding, knowledge work and science. The launch post leads with benchmark rankings. We didn't check those, so we'll skip them.

The part that matters for a chat UI is quieter. Neon can produce up to 1M tokens in a single answer, but changing the model ID alone doesn't enable that. Any one request still stops at 65,536 tokens of thinking plus output. Here's how the longer answers work with the AI SDK, and two things we only noticed once we ran it.

What the docs say

From What's new in Gemini 4 Neon and the release notes:

  • Price: $3.00 per 1M input tokens and $15.00 per 1M output tokens, thinking included, flat across the window. Cached input is $0.15 per 1M (a 95% discount from implicit caching).
  • Paid tier only. Unlike Hydrogen, there's no free tier.
  • Thinking levels: low, medium, high (the default) and xhigh. minimal is rejected.
  • One shared window: input, thinking and output share 1,048,576 tokens.

The long decode guide explains the rest. Generation runs in hops of up to 64K tokens. If a hop hits that cap and budget is left, the response ends with finishReason: CONTINUATION and an encrypted continuationToken. You send the same request again with that token and don't add the partial output to contents, because the token carries the state. When the whole max_output_tokens budget is used, the response ends with MAX_TOKENS instead.

Google is also clear about when this is worth it. Chat, Q&A and summaries finish well under 32K tokens and don't need it. It's for hard reasoning and "write the whole thing" jobs like a full migration spec. So we made it a per-message toggle, not the default.

SDK support

@ai-sdk/google 4.0.123 (November 20) added the gemini-4-neon ID with xhigh. Long decode support itself landed earlier, in 4.0.95: the provider continues CONTINUATION hops for you, sums usage, and exposes initialPromptTokenCount. We used ai@7.0.179 and @ai-sdk/google@4.0.124.

The route 

// app/api/chat/route.ts
import { streamText, convertToModelMessages, type UIMessage } from 'ai';
import { google } from '@ai-sdk/google';

export const maxDuration = 900; // hops can take minutes; check your host's limit

export type ChatMeta = {
  finishReason?: string;
  contextTokens?: number;     // what the conversation actually occupies
  billedInputTokens?: number; // summed over every hop, for cost only
  continuationToken?: string;
};

export async function POST(req: Request) {
  const { messages, long = false, continuationToken }: {
    messages: UIMessage[]; long?: boolean; continuationToken?: string;
  } = await req.json();

  const result = streamText({
    model: google('gemini-4-neon'),
    messages: await convertToModelMessages(messages),
    // Above 65,536 the provider runs the 64K hops for you
    maxOutputTokens: long ? 262_144 : undefined,
    providerOptions: {
      google: {
        thinkingConfig: { thinkingLevel: long ? 'high' : 'medium', includeThoughts: true },
        ...(continuationToken && { continuationToken }),
      },
    },
  });

  return result.toUIMessageStreamResponse<UIMessage<ChatMeta>>({
    sendReasoning: true,
    messageMetadata: ({ part }) => {
      if (part.type !== 'finish-step') return;
      const g = part.providerMetadata?.google as
        { initialPromptTokenCount?: number; continuationToken?: string } | undefined;
      const input = part.usage.inputTokens ?? 0;
      const output = part.usage.outputTokens ?? 0;
      return {
        finishReason: part.finishReason,
        billedInputTokens: input,
        contextTokens: (g?.initialPromptTokenCount ?? input) + output,
        continuationToken: g?.continuationToken,
      };
    },
  });
}

What the test showed

Our mock replaces fetch and streams SSE chunks shaped like the docs' examples. It isn't a captured Gemini response. We drove the route the way useChat does.

  1. Without maxOutputTokens, the answer just stops. One request, finishReason: 'length', half a spec. The UI shows it as finished unless you check.
  2. With 262,144, the hops are invisible. Three requests went out. The second and third carried the previous continuationToken, and contents was identical each time. The first hop was all thinking with empty text, which the docs call normal. The client got one reasoning block and one text block, as if it were a single response.
  3. usage.inputTokens is not your context size. It came back as 199,608, the sum of each hop's input (1,000 + 66,536 + 132,072), because every hop re-reads everything generated so far. The real context was 162,072. The docs warn about this. If your app trims or summarises history when a token count gets close to the limit, feed it initialPromptTokenCount plus output, not inputTokens, or it'll compact far too early.

For the cut-off case we added a Continue button. It sends the original prompt plus the token and a bigger budget. regenerate already drops the partial answer from the request, which is what Google asks for:

{status === 'ready' && meta?.finishReason === 'length' && meta.continuationToken && (
  <button onClick={() => {
    setCarry(carry + textOf(last!)); // the new message holds only the rest
    regenerate({ body: { long: true, continuationToken: meta.continuationToken } });
  }}>
    Hit the token limit. Continue
  </button>
)}

The rest of the component is a normal useChat list with a details block for reasoning. We type-checked it and ran this flow through the AI SDK Chat class: one user message went out, the token reached Gemini, and the displayed text joined up.

Honest limits

  • We didn't call the real API. Before you ship, run one real long request and compare the hop count and usage with what you log.
  • Dropped streams don't resume from checkpoints. After the first 64K on Neon, the stream sends a checkpoint token about every 5,000 tokens, and Google's REST loop resumes from the last one. In our test, a stream cut after a checkpoint ended as finishReason: 'interrupted' with no token in the metadata, and the text after the checkpoint stayed in the message. With this SDK version you resend the request instead.
  • The resumed message is only the tail. Our carry fixes the display, but the stored history holds just the second part. Merge them before the next turn.
  • Time limits. Google suggests HTTP timeouts of at least 15 minutes, and the server closes a stream after 20. Check your host's function time limit before relying on maxDuration. For truly long jobs, Google recommends background execution on the Interactions API, which this route doesn't use.
  • Cost. Every hop is billed, including thinking-only hops. Repeated input in each hop gets the 95% cache discount, but if the model uses the whole 262,144-token budget, that's about $3.90 of output for one answer.

Sources

  • Introducing Gemini 4 Neon, Google
  • What's new in Gemini 4 Neon
  • Gemini API release notes
  • Long decode and long decode with generateContent
  • @ai-sdk/google 4.0.123 and 4.0.95

If you'd rather not hand-build the reasoning block and message list, Cuelark UI has shadcn-style components for AI chat that work with this setup.

title: Inkling 2 Mini Is a 26B Open-Weights Model That Runs on Your Laptop
description:
Thinking Machines Lab released Inkling 2 Mini on November 20, and it is the most interesting local model launch in a while. It is a multimodal open-weights model with 26.4 billion total parameters and only 3.4 billion active per token — and the whole checkpoint is about 20GB, small enough to run on a laptop.

The trick is looping. Inkling 2 Mini has 24 decoder layers in four blocks of six. The first block runs once, the two middle blocks run three times each, and the final block runs once, so each token passes through 48 layer applications even though only 24 layers are stored. It was also trained natively in 4-bit precision — 20 layers in NVFP4, the last four in MXFP8 — and the released checkpoint keeps that exact layout, so there is no conversion loss.

On benchmarks it leads every open-weights model under 100B total parameters on DeepSWE v1.1 (48.2%) and Vals Index v2.2 (46.5%), and it beats Qwen3.8-27B — the model most local coding setups default to — on DeepSWE, SWE-bench Pro v2 Hard, SWE-bench Multilingual, SWE-bench Verified and Vibe Code Bench. Stanford researchers also measured intelligence per joule: Inkling 2 Mini scored 0.703 on an NVIDIA DGX Spark, against 0.430 for Qwen3.6-35B-A3B.

For local inference, the official targets are a single NVIDIA DGX Spark or Apple silicon with 32GB or more of memory. It works with Hugging Face transformers, SGLang, vLLM, llama.cpp GGUF versions, Ollama and MLX, and it is Apache 2.0 licensed, so you can fine-tune it and build it into products. The demos are the fun part: researchers ran it offline on a MacBook Pro in airplane mode during a flight and built a playable flight simulator in a few minutes, and one offline MacBook powered all 20 residents of "Thinkyville", a tiny pixel town.

If you have a 32GB Mac or a DGX Spark-class machine, this is now the local model to beat. The weights are free on Hugging Face, and you can also try it in the Tinker playground without downloading anything.

Read the full article with all the details on Rohan Tech Official: https://rohantechofficial.com/tech-news/inkling-2-mini-local-ai-model/

title: Run SenseNova-Loop-9B on Consumer GPUs: Deploying the 9B Multimodal Vision Model That Outperforms 27B with Local Loop Reasoning in 2026
description:
Published by PixelBrain Studio Engineering Labs · Open-Source AI Architecture Series · 42 Min Master Implementation Blueprint

1. Executive Summary: The Recurrent Loop Architecture Revolution

For the past three years, the open-source large language model ecosystem has been trapped in a linear scaling trap: to achieve deeper multi-step reasoning, mathematical proofing, and complex visual scene understanding, developers were forced to double or quadruple parameter counts. Running a state-of-the-art vision-language model meant provisioning heavy 27B, 32B, or 70B models requiring dual RTX 4090s or expensive cloud A100/H100 clusters costing upwards of $600 to $1,800 every month.

In late 2026, SenseTime and the open-source AI community upended this brute-force paradigm with the release of SenseNova-Loop-9B.

Instead of stacking dozens of static transformer layers, SenseNova-Loop introduces a Recurrent Loop Reasoning Architecture:

  1. Dynamic Recurrent Computation: Internal hidden states are routed through recurrent attention loops across complex reasoning steps, allowing a compact 9.0 Billion parameter model to dynamically expand its effective computational depth to 14.6B–27B equivalent capacity on demand.
  2. Massive 512K Native Context Window: Out of the box, SenseNova-Loop natively ingests and cross-examines 500+ pages of dense legal briefs, engineering schematics, or multi-hour video transcript frames without context fragmentation.
  3. Lossless Multimodal Vision-Language Projection: Leveraging a specialized mmproj-F16 vision encoder (~918MB), the model parses high-resolution infographics, architectural blueprints, scientific plots, and dense multilingual OCR with sub-millimeter precision.
  4. Consumer Hardware Sovereignty: Fully quantized Q4_K_M weights occupy just 5.63 GB of VRAM, allowing single-developer studios and solo operators to deploy enterprise-grade multimodal AI on entry-level 6GB, 8GB, or 12GB GPUs (RTX 3060, RTX 4060, or Apple Silicon MacBooks) with zero recurring token fees.

In this comprehensive production deployment guide, we walk through the exact steps to build, configure, and orchestrate SenseNova-Loop-9B locally, expose an OpenAI-compatible /v1/chat/completions API server, integrate it into sovereign automated pipelines, and benchmark its performance against closed proprietary models.

2. Hardware Matrix & Quantization Selection Guide

Understanding quantization trade-offs is essential to maximizing tokens-per-second while keeping latency minimal. Below is the audited memory footprint and performance matrix for SenseNova-Loop-9B across consumer hardware tiers:

Quantization Format File Size Recommended VRAM Context Capacity (4K / 32K / 128K) Target Hardware Tier
Q3_K_M 4.64 GB 6 GB 4K–16K Context RTX 3060 Laptop, GTX 1660 Ti, M1/M2 8GB
Q4_K_M (Recommended) 5.63 GB 8 GB 16K–64K Context RTX 4060 8GB, RTX 3070, Apple M-Series 16GB
Q5_K_M 6.82 GB 10 GB 32K–128K Context RTX 3080 10GB, RTX 4070 12GB
Q8_0 (Near FP16 Quality) 9.54 GB 12 GB–16 GB Full 512K Context (with FlashAttention) RTX 4070 Ti Super, RTX 4080, RTX 3090/4090
mmproj-F16 (Vision Module) 918 MB (Loaded into VRAM) Synchronous 16MP Image Ingestion Dedicated Vision Tensor Layer

For developers operating without dedicated local desktop GPUs, spinning up an unthrottled Linux KVM VPS on Hostinger Cloud VPS provides dedicated NVMe scratch disks and high-bandwidth IPv4/IPv6 networking starting under $8/month, allowing you to host private API endpoints accessible across all your remote agents.

3. Compiling the Custom llama.cpp Engine with Loop Support

Because SenseNova-Loop employs non-linear recurrent token routing, standard upstream builds of llama.cpp will throw an assertion error on layer unrolling. You must build the optimized fork supporting dynamic loop layers.

3.1 Linux / Ubuntu / Debian CUDA Compilation: 

git clone https://github.com/terasut-num/llama.cpp-SenseNova-loop.git
cd llama.cpp-SenseNova-loop

mkdir build && cd build
cmake .. -DGGML_CUDA=ON -DGGML_CUDA_FA_ALL=ON -DCMAKE_BUILD_TYPE=Release

cmake --build . --config Release -j$(nproc)

./bin/llama-cli --version

3.2 Windows (MSVC + CUDA 12.x) Build Instructions:

For Windows operators using PowerShell:

git clone https://github.com/terasut-num/llama.cpp-SenseNova-loop.git
cd llama.cpp-SenseNova-loop
cmake -B build -DGGML_CUDA=ON -DCMAKE_BUILD_TYPE=Release
cmake --build build --config Release -j 12

3.3 Containerized Production Deployment: Dockerfile

For sysadmins who prefer immutable infrastructure, deploy via Docker:

FROM nvidia/cuda:12.4.1-devel-ubuntu22.04 AS builder

RUN apt-get update && apt-get install -y git build-essential cmake

WORKDIR /app
RUN git clone https://github.com/terasut-num/llama.cpp-SenseNova-loop.git .
RUN mkdir build && cd build &&     cmake .. -DGGML_CUDA=ON -DGGML_CUDA_FA_ALL=ON -DCMAKE_BUILD_TYPE=Release &&     cmake --build . --config Release -j$(nproc)

FROM nvidia/cuda:12.4.1-runtime-ubuntu22.04

RUN apt-get update && apt-get install -y libgomp1 curl && rm -rf /var/lib/apt/lists/*
WORKDIR /app
COPY --from=builder /app/build/bin/llama-server /app/llama-server

EXPOSE 8080
ENTRYPOINT ["/app/llama-server"]

4. Downloading Verified Model Weights & Vision Adapters

The official community GGUF repository provides pre-quantized weights ready for single-file ingestion:

mkdir -p ~/models/sensenova-loop-9b
cd ~/models/sensenova-loop-9b

curl -L -o sensenova-loop-9b-q4_k_m.gguf   "https://huggingface.co/guideboardlabs/SenseNova-Loop-9B-GGUF/resolve/main/SenseNova-Loop-9B-Q4_K_M.gguf"

curl -L -o mmproj-model-f16.gguf   "https://huggingface.co/AtomicChat/SenseNova-Loop-9B-GGUF/resolve/main/mmproj-SenseNova-Loop-F16.gguf"

Verify checksum integrity to prevent corruption during large transfers:

sha256sum sensenova-loop-9b-q4_k_m.gguf

5. Deploying the High-Throughput OpenAI-Compatible Server

To allow drop-in compatibility with existing AI frameworks (LangChain, LlamaIndex, n8n, AutoGen, and Claude-like chat interfaces), launch the native llama-server with GPU layer offloading and vision support:

./bin/llama-server   --model ~/models/sensenova-loop-9b/sensenova-loop-9b-q4_k_m.gguf   --mmproj ~/models/sensenova-loop-9b/mmproj-model-f16.gguf   --n-gpu-layers 35   --ctx-size 32768   --batch-size 2048   --ubatch-size 512   --threads 8   --host 0.0.0.0   --port 8080   --flash-attn   --parallel 2   --api-key "sk-pixelbrain-local-sensenova"

Server Flag Optimization Breakdown:

  • --n-gpu-layers 35: Fully offloads all recurrent attention blocks into VRAM, leaving only scratch CPU buffers for initial prompt ingestion.
  • --ctx-size 32768: Establishes a 32K working context window (~45 pages of documentation). Expand up to 524288 (512K) on 16GB+ VRAM hardware.
  • --flash-attn: Drastically reduces memory consumption during long multi-image prompt sequences.
  • --parallel 2: Enables simultaneous dual-request execution without blocking the inference loop.

6. Real-World Vision Inference: Autonomous Document & Receipt Parsing

Unlike standard text LLMs, SenseNova-Loop-9B can inspect dense financial reports, complex user interface screenshots, and dirty handwriting in a single inference call.

6.1 Synchronous Extraction Script (parse_vision.py): 

import base64
import requests
import json

def encode_image(image_path):
    with open(image_path, "rb") as image_file:
        return base64.b64encode(image_file.read()).decode('utf-8')

def analyze_multimodal_document(image_path, prompt_text):
    base64_image = encode_image(image_path)

    headers = {
        "Content-Type": "application/json",
        "Authorization": "Bearer sk-pixelbrain-local-sensenova"
    }

    payload = {
        "model": "sensenova-loop-9b",
        "messages": [
            {
                "role": "system",
                "content": "You are an expert OCR and financial data extraction assistant. Output strict JSON only."
            },
            {
                "role": "user",
                "content": [
                    {"type": "text", "text": prompt_text},
                    {
                        "type": "image_url",
                        "image_url": {
                            "url": f"data:image/jpeg;base64,{base64_image}"
                        }
                    }
                ]
            }
        ],
        "temperature": 0.1,
        "max_tokens": 1500
    }

    response = requests.post("http://localhost:8080/v1/chat/completions", headers=headers, json=payload)
    return response.json()

if __name__ == "__main__":
    result = analyze_multimodal_document(
        "sample_financial_statement.png",
        "Extract total revenue, net operating income, EBITDA, and fiscal year into a validated JSON object."
    )
    print(json.dumps(result, indent=2))

6.2 High-Throughput Batch Ingestion with Asyncio (batch_ocr_pipeline.py):

For automated production pipelines processing hundreds of scanned invoices per hour:

import asyncio
import aiohttp
import base64
import os
import glob
import json

SERVER_URL = "http://localhost:8080/v1/chat/completions"
API_KEY = "sk-pixelbrain-local-sensenova"

async def process_single_image(session, sem, image_path):
    async with sem:
        with open(image_path, "rb") as f:
            b64_str = base64.b64encode(f.read()).decode('utf-8')

        payload = {
            "model": "sensenova-loop-9b",
            "messages": [
                {"role": "system", "content": "Extract invoice items, vendor name, tax, and total. Strict JSON."},
                {"role": "user", "content": [
                    {"type": "text", "text": "Parse this document:"},
                    {"type": "image_url", "image_url": {"url": f"data:image/jpeg;base64,{b64_str}"} }
                ]}
            ],
            "temperature": 0.05
        }

        headers = {"Authorization": f"Bearer {API_KEY}", "Content-Type": "application/json"}
        try:
            async with session.post(SERVER_URL, json=payload, headers=headers, timeout=60) as resp:
                data = await resp.json()
                content = data["choices"][0]["message"]["content"]
                return {"file": image_path, "status": "success", "data": json.loads(content)}
        except Exception as e:
            return {"file": image_path, "status": "error", "error": str(e)}

async def main():
    images = glob.glob("invoices/*.jpg") + glob.glob("invoices/*.png")
    sem = asyncio.Semaphore(4) # Limit concurrency to match GPU compute capacity
    async with aiohttp.ClientSession() as session:
        tasks = [process_single_image(session, sem, img) for img in images]
        results = await asyncio.gather(*tasks)
        with open("batch_ocr_results.json", "w", encoding="utf-8") as out:
            json.dump(results, out, indent=2)
    print(f"Batch processing completed for {len(images)} documents.")

if __name__ == "__main__":
    asyncio.run(main())

6.3 Cross-Document Multimodal Reasoning & Sequence Alignment

A recurring bottleneck with small vision models is their inability to maintain consistency across multiple consecutive images. In multi-page contract audits, a clause stated on Page 1 often defines the liability cap evaluated on Page 7.

SenseNova-Loop-9B solves this via its 512K context buffer and recurrent cross-attention. When multiple images are submitted inside a single user turn:

  1. The mmproj-F16 vision adapter encodes each image into separate visual token embeddings.
  2. The recurrent loop passes visual tokens through the shared hidden state without downsampling resolution.
  3. The model constructs a unified spatial mental graph, comparing tables across different pages without losing column alignment.

8. Benchmark Comparison: SenseNova-Loop-9B vs. 27B Competitors

We evaluated SenseNova-Loop-9B across standard multimodal and mathematical reasoning benchmarks against popular 27B open-source weights and commercial APIs:

Benchmark / Capability SenseNova-Loop-9B (Q4_K_M) Qwen3.8-27B (FP16) Gemma-2-27B (Q4_K_M) GPT-4o Vision (Commercial)

title: Cached Input Discounts: The Hidden Lever in Agent Costs — What It Is and Why It Matters
description:
Short answer: For cached input token discount, the decision usually turns on fee shape, model coverage and deployment model — not the headline rate. TENSORAXIS publishes per-token rates behind one OpenAI-compatible key; self-hosted options like LiteLLM trade a platform fee for operational work. All figures below are dated and source-cited.

Disclosure: TENSORAXIS is the product we operate. This is an editorial comparison built from public sources, not an independent benchmark or a third-party user review. Competitor figures are attributed and dated; verify all rates on vendor sites before deciding.

A developer-focused look at cached input token discount. Figures are attributed and dated; skip to the table if you want the short version.

What the published figures actually say

Some providers price cached input up to 50% off; for agent loops with a fixed system prompt this matters more than the headline token rate. (Source: llmapi.ai/how-we-compared-20-openrouter-alternatives)

Published per-1M rates include claude-opus-4-8 at $0.42 in / $2.13 out, gemini-3.5-flash at $0.19 / $1.11, gpt-5.6-terra at $1.50 / $2.00, and domestic glm-5.3 at ¥2.71 / ¥9.49. (Source: tensoraxis.ai/en/models (verified 2026-11-18))

With an OpenAI-compatible endpoint, migration is a base_url and api_key change; tool calling, structured output, embeddings and streaming are where compatibility diverges. (Source: editorial synthesis of public gateway docs (2026-11))

Why does this matter for my workload?

The same model can be priced and routed differently across gateways. Normalise everything to cost per million input and output tokens for the models you actually call, then add the layer fee at your real volume. For a worked comparison see the Sources section.

How do I compare two gateways honestly?

  1. Normalise the unit to per-1M input/output tokens.
  2. Add the layer fee at your real volume, not the headline volume.
  3. Include cached-input discounts where available.
  4. Price the failover route at the rate of the model that serves it.
  5. Count migration effort against the monthly saving.

title: On-device AI agents got real this month. Where a small local model beats a big remote one.
description:
Three releases from October point the same way:

  • Liquid AI LFM2.5-24B-A2B: an open mixture-of-experts model built for on-device agents. 24B total, 2B active per token. Liquid measured 184 tokens/s on an Apple M5 Max.
  • NVIDIA Nemotron 3.5 Bolt E4B: a compact model for local assistants, about 4B effective parameters.
  • Liquid AI LFM3: a family of small text, vision, audio and decision models, each picked by what it does and where it runs.

The "2B active" part is the trick. The model knows a lot (24B parameters), but each token only uses a small part of it, so it runs at a speed a laptop or a good phone can handle.

Where a local model wins

Not on raw quality. A frontier model in a data centre is still better at hard reasoning. A local model wins on everything around the answer:

1. Privacy by construction. The text never leaves the device. For a parking app, think of a driver's location history, or an owner's photos of their home driveway. "We don't send it" is a stronger promise than "we send it, but securely".

2. It works with no signal. I wrote about a trip where the signal dropped halfway through. Basement car parks are exactly where you lose network. A feature that needs the cloud fails at the moment it's needed.

3. No per-call cost. Once it's on the device, a thousand calls cost the same as one. That changes which features are worth building: things like checking every input or classifying every photo.

4. Latency without a network round trip. For small, frequent decisions this adds up quickly.

Where it doesn't

  • App size and memory. Even small models are hundreds of MB to a few GB. That's a big download for a parking app.
  • Battery and heat. Fine for occasional calls, harder for continuous ones.
  • Hard reasoning. Planning a multi-step task or writing long text is still better done remotely.
  • Updates. A model shipped inside an app updates when the app does.

The pattern I'd use: local first, remote when it matters

Use the small local model for the many small decisions, and the big remote model for the few hard ones:

Task Where
"Is this photo a parking spot?" Local
"Does this message mention a payment problem?" Local
Voice to text for search Local
Explain a disputed charge Remote
Plan a multi-stop trip Remote

The local model can also decide when to call the remote one, which is a nice use for the small decision models in LFM3.

What I'd tell you before you start

On-device AI isn't a smaller version of cloud AI. It's good at different things: private, offline, free per call, and instant. Pick the features where those matter, and keep the hard thinking in the cloud.

Sources: Liquid AI blog (Oct 13 and Oct 27, 2026) and NVIDIA model card (Oct 23, 2026), via "AI Model Releases: October 2026 Tracker", Digital Applied. Speed figures are the vendors' own.
