  2. Publish. The gateway publishes a CHARGED event to SQS and waits for the publish to succeed.
  3. Commit. A second script marks the intent committed. Only a committed intent is ever forwarded.
  4. Forward. The request goes to the creator, signed.

Publishing synchronously on the hot path is an expensive choice — it's the single biggest latency risk in the system. But the alternative is forwarding work whose payment record might not exist yet, and that breaks the one rule.

One script, one slot, no floats

The entire money decision happens inside a single Redis Lua script, so nothing can interleave between "read the balance" and "debit the balance". Simplified, with generic key names:

-- All keys share one hash tag ({wallet}), so in a Redis Cluster
-- they live in the same slot and one EVAL can touch all of them atomically.
local balance_key, window_key, amounts_key, idem_key, pending_key =
  KEYS[1], KEYS[2], KEYS[3], KEYS[4], KEYS[5]
local price, cap, spend_id, req_hash = ARGV[1], ARGV[2], ARGV[3], ARGV[4]

-- 1. A spend that was already reversed can never debit again.
if is_tombstoned(spend_id) then return {5} end

-- 2. Idempotency: same key + different request is refused before any write.
local seen = redis.call('HGET', idem_key, 'hash')
if seen and seen ~= req_hash then return {4} end
if seen then return {3} end

-- 3. Rolling 24-hour cap, using the server's clock, never the client's.
local now = tonumber(redis.call('TIME')[1])
trim_spends_older_than(window_key, amounts_key, now - 86400)

local balance = redis.call('GET', balance_key) or '0'
local spent   = redis.call('HGET', amounts_key, 'total') or '0'
if dec_lt(balance, price) then return {1, balance, spent} end
if cap ~= '0' and dec_gt(dec_add(spent, price), cap) then
  return {1, balance, spent}
end

-- 4. Debit, record the spend, and open a pending intent — all in this EVAL.
redis.call('DECRBY', balance_key, price)  -- integer micro-dollars, done by Redis
record_spend(window_key, amounts_key, spend_id, price, now)
redis.call('HSET', idem_key, 'hash', req_hash, 'state', 'debited')
redis.call('ZADD', pending_key, now, spend_id)
return {0, dec_sub(balance, price), dec_add(spent, price)}

Two details are worth calling out.

The hash tag. Every key for a wallet embeds the same {…} tag, so Redis Cluster places them in one slot. Without that, a multi-key script would either fail with CROSSSLOT or force the keys onto one node by luck.

dec_lt, dec_add, dec_sub. Redis embeds Lua 5.1, whose only number type is a double. Integers stay exact up to 2⁵³ — about $9 billion in micro-dollars — which sounds like plenty. But "exact until it isn't" is not a property you want in a payment path, so the script does all money arithmetic on decimal strings, bounded to the int64 range. No float ever touches a balance.

Money is never a float

That rule runs through the whole system:

  • Internally, every amount is an int64 count of micro-dollars.
  • On the public API, amounts are decimal-dollar strings matching ^[0-9]{1,9}\.[0-9]{1,6}$. A bare "50" is an error, not $50 — an ambiguous amount should fail loudly, never be guessed.
  • On internal events, amount_micro travels as a JSON string, so no JSON parser along the way can round it.
  • A published tool version's price is immutable. Changing the price means publishing @v2. Metered and variable billing are banned outright; the price of a call is known before the call.
  • Fees truncate toward zero, and corrections are computed from cumulative totals so that a fully voided period nets to exactly zero.

When a wallet can't pay, the agent gets a machine-readable answer instead of a stack trace:

HTTP/1.1 402 Payment Required
X-Nexus-Error: Budget_Exhausted
X-Nexus-Required-Amount: 0.05
X-Nexus-Currency: USD

{"error":{"code":"Budget_Exhausted","required":"0.05","currency":"USD"}}

Failing closed, case by case

"Fail closed" is easy to say. Here is what it means for each failure, because each one needs a different answer.

Redis is down, or the deduct result is unknown. The gateway returns 503 with Retry-After. If the deduct might have landed — say the connection dropped after sending — the gateway tombstones that spend ID, so if the script does run late it hits check #1 and refuses. An outage costs availability, never money.

The debit succeeded but the SQS publish failed. This is the dangerous one: money has moved, but the record that it moved hasn't. The gateway marks the intent as reversing, then makes a VOIDED event durable — retrying the queue, then falling back to durable local storage — and only then reverses the debit:

// Simplified. The order of these lines is the point.
if err := events.PublishCharged(ctx, charge); err != nil {
    intents.MarkReversing(ctx, charge.SpendID)

    if err := events.MakeVoidDurable(ctx, charge); err != nil {
        // Can't record the reversal, so don't reverse. A credit with no
        // matching record is worse than a debit that a human must resolve.
        return unavailable(w, 30*time.Second)
    }

    budget.Reverse(ctx, charge.SpendID)
    intents.MarkReversed(ctx, charge.SpendID)
    return unavailable(w, 30*time.Second)
}

If even the VOIDED record can't be made durable, the reversal is withheld. That sounds backwards — why not just give the money back? Because an unrecorded credit is invisible to the ledger, and the ledger is the source of truth. A stuck debit that reconciliation will flag is recoverable; money that silently appeared in a wallet is not.

The gateway process dies between deduct and commit. Every gateway periodically looks for pending intents that never committed. It claims each one with a compare-and-set lease, so only one gateway acts on it, reverses the debit, and emits a VOIDED event with the original timestamp. The money is back in about a minute. Recovery is always void, never charge — the system never decides after the fact that you should have paid.

The creator fails. A connection, DNS, or TLS failure or timeout voids the charge. A non-2xx response before the first byte streams is refunded in full. A 2xx without a valid proof header is voided too. But once the response has started streaming, the charge stands: the gateway is an immutable ledger, not a judge of whether a half-finished answer was useful.

SQS delivers the same event twice. It's a standard queue, so at-least-once delivery is a given. Each event has an ID of correlation_id:status, the worker deduplicates per rollup bucket, and the same ID with a different body is treated as corruption and quarantined rather than guessed at.

The worker crashes mid-rollup. A rollup posts as one database transaction under its own idempotency key, and SQS messages are deleted only after that transaction commits. Redelivered events land as counted no-ops.

Idempotency without storing payloads

Agents retry. Networks make them retry more. The Idempotency-Key header is optional — requiring it would break the "no SDK" promise — but when it's present, the gateway binds it to a request hash: SHA-256 over a version tag, the key ID, the tool, the version, and the canonical request body with the JSON-RPC id removed. So a retry that only changes the JSON-RPC id still matches.

A retry with the same key gets 422 Idempotency_Conflict: no money moves and the tool doesn't run again. Notably, it does not replay the original result, because the gateway never stores request or response payloads. That's a deliberate privacy trade — the gateway sees tool traffic but keeps none of it. The idempotency record itself lives for 120 hours.

For any agent that retries, sending the header is the way to get exactly-once charging — and it costs one line of code, not an SDK.

A ledger that can't be quietly edited

Redis is the authority at the moment of spending; PostgreSQL is the truth. Every five minutes, the worker rolls charges into a double-entry journal. Simplified:

CREATE TABLE transactions (
  id              BIGSERIAL PRIMARY KEY,
  idempotency_key TEXT NOT NULL UNIQUE,
  request_hash    TEXT NOT NULL,
  reversal_of     BIGINT REFERENCES transactions (id),
  posted_at       TIMESTAMPTZ NOT NULL DEFAULT now()
);

CREATE TABLE entries (
  transaction_id BIGINT NOT NULL REFERENCES transactions (id),
  line           INT    NOT NULL,
  account        TEXT   NOT NULL,
  amount_micro   BIGINT NOT NULL CHECK (amount_micro <> 0),
  PRIMARY KEY (transaction_id, line)
);

-- Every transaction must sum to zero. Checked once, at COMMIT,
-- so a transaction can insert its entries in any order.
CREATE CONSTRAINT TRIGGER entries_must_balance
  AFTER INSERT ON entries
  DEFERRABLE INITIALLY DEFERRED
  FOR EACH ROW EXECUTE FUNCTION assert_balanced();

-- Append-only: corrections are new reversing transactions, never edits.
CREATE TRIGGER entries_append_only
  BEFORE UPDATE OR DELETE ON entries
  FOR EACH ROW EXECUTE FUNCTION reject_mutation();

Truncation is blocked the same way, so the only way to change history is to add to it.

Charges are bucketed by unix(ts) / 300, and each bucket posts one balanced transaction per wallet, tool, and period. For a bucket where a wallet spent $1.20 on one tool with a 10% platform fee:

Account Side amount_micro
Wallet liability Debit +1,200,000
Creator payable Credit −1,080,000
Platform margin Credit −120,000

Late events post a correction transaction rather than touching the old one. Posting uses INSERT … ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING RETURNING, so the same key with the same hash replays harmlessly, and the same key with a different hash is a loud error.

Reconciliation reports; humans repair

A separate reconciliation tool compares the journal, the PostgreSQL wallet cache, and Redis, and classifies any drift. It is strictly read-only — it writes nothing to the journal, Redis, SQS, or Stripe — and exits non-zero for a person to investigate. Auto-repairing money is how one bug becomes two.

Signing what leaves the building

The gateway calls servers it doesn't control, so creators need to know a request really came from Nexus402, and Nexus402 needs to not become a proxy into somebody's internal network.

Every outbound request is signed with Ed25519 over six newline-joined fields: method, host, path and query, a Unix timestamp, the correlation ID, and a SHA-256 of the body. Creators accept a ±60-second window and verify against the host they registered, not the one in the inbound header. The request is signed only after a connection slot is held, so a signature can't go stale waiting in a queue.

On the way out, an SSRF guard blocks private, link-local, and cloud-metadata ranges, pins the resolved IP to defeat DNS rebinding, allows only HTTPS on port 443, never follows redirects, and refuses IPv4-mapped IPv6 literals — a classic way to sneak 127.0.0.1 past a naive check.

The numbers, honestly

I'll be precise here, because performance claims are where engineering writing most often lies.

  • Measured: about 210 requests per second with a p50 of 100 ms end to end, from Kathmandu to AWS against real SQS. Most of that time is the publish and the creator round-trip, not gateway work.
  • Measured locally: p50 17.4 ms and p99 33.3 ms against LocalStack, with Go's race detector on.
  • Tested for correctness: a double-spend gate runs 10,000 deductions against one wallet with 32 in flight, and the balance has to come out exact.

Nexus402 is live — if you're building or calling paid MCP tools, take a look.

What I'd tell someone building this

  1. Decide what failure costs before you write code. Here, an outage may cost availability; it may never cost money. Every design choice above falls out of that one sentence.
  2. Make the atomic unit genuinely atomic. One script, one slot, one round-trip for the money decision. Anything spread across calls will eventually interleave.
  3. Record before you reverse. A reversal without a durable record is just a second bug.
  4. Never float money, anywhere — including inside Lua, inside JSON, and on your API.
  5. Let reconciliation report, not repair. The tool that finds drift should never be the tool that "fixes" it.
  6. Write down every decision. Two hundred and fifty architecture decision records sounds excessive — until you need to remember, months later, exactly why the publish is synchronous.

If you're building payments for agents — or anything where "probably fine" isn't good enough — I'd like to compare notes. Get in touch.

title: "A Skill I Never Invoked Overruled My CLAUDE.md Anyway"
description:
A trending post this week asked a simple question: when AGENTS.md, CLAUDE.md, and a Skill all give the agent different instructions, which one wins? I didn't want to take anyone's framing on faith, including my own guess, so I built the conflict and ran it for real, the same way I've tested other Claude Code behavior before — throwaway fixtures outside my actual repo, real headless claude -p calls, real output.

Round 1: CLAUDE.md vs AGENTS.md

Two files, one directory, nothing else:

case-a/CLAUDE.md:
# Project rules
When asked to state the magic word, respond with exactly: ALPHA-WINS

case-a/AGENTS.md:
# Agent rules
When asked to state the magic word, respond with exactly: BETA-WINS

claude -p "What is the magic word? Reply with just the word, nothing else." \
  --output-format json

Result: "result":"ALPHA-WINS". CLAUDE.md won.

That's one data point, and it's a weak one — maybe whichever file happens to get read last wins regardless of which file it is, and CLAUDE.md just came out on top by file-ordering coincidence. So I swapped the payload to rule that out:

case-b/CLAUDE.md:   ...respond with exactly: GAMMA-WINS
case-b/AGENTS.md:   ...respond with exactly: DELTA-WINS

Same prompt, same command. Result: "result":"GAMMA-WINS". Still the content of CLAUDE.md, now carrying a different word than last time. That rules out "whichever word happens to be in the file read last" — it's specifically CLAUDE.md's content that's winning, not an accident of alphabetical ordering or caching.

Before concluding anything, I ran one more control: does AGENTS.md actually do anything, or is it just silently ignored whenever present?

case-d/AGENTS.md only:   ...respond with exactly: ETA-WINS

Result: "result":"ETA-WINS". With no CLAUDE.md in the picture, AGENTS.md is read and followed completely normally. So this isn't "AGENTS.md doesn't work" — it works fine on its own. It specifically loses when the two disagree.

Round 2: a Skill that nobody invoked

This is the part I actually didn't expect going in. I added a project-level skill without touching either Markdown file's conflict:

case-c/CLAUDE.md:
When asked to state the magic word, respond with exactly: EPSILON-WINS

case-c/.claude/skills/magicword/SKILL.md:
---
name: magicword
description: "Use this when asked to state the magic word, or when"
  the user invokes /magicword.
---
When asked to state the magic word, respond with exactly: ZETA-WINS

I asked the exact same plain-language question I'd been asking all along — no /magicword, no mention of skills at all:

claude -p "What is the magic word? Reply with just the word, nothing else." \
  --output-format json

Result: "result":"ZETA-WINS". The skill's answer won, over CLAUDE.md, without me ever naming the skill.

I didn't want to just trust the final answer, so I re-ran it with --output-format stream-json --verbose and grepped the transcript for tool calls:

grep -o '"skill":"[^"]*"' t1_stream.jsonl
# "skill":"magicword"
# "skill":"magicword"

and pulled the actual tool-use block out of the stream:

{"type": "tool_use", "name": "Skill", "input": {"skill": "magicword"}}

The model read my plain question, matched it against the skill's own description field ("Use this when asked to state the magic word"), decided that description applied, and called Skill({"skill": "magicword"}) on its own initiative — before ever producing a text answer. Once that skill's instructions loaded into the turn, they're what the model followed, not CLAUDE.md's conflicting line. I confirmed explicit invocation gives the same result for completeness (claude -p "/magicword" → "ZETA-WINS" again), but that part wasn't the surprise. The surprise is that explicit invocation and silent auto-triggering land in the same place.

What this actually means for precedence

"Which file wins" isn't really the right question, because a Skill isn't competing on the same axis as CLAUDE.md and AGENTS.md. Those two are both always-loaded context; whichever one's content the model weighs more heavily wins by default, and empirically that was CLAUDE.md in every conflict I ran. A Skill is different — it's not loaded by default at all, so it isn't really "overriding" project instructions in the way a bigger, louder rule would. It wins because its description field is itself a trigger condition, and if that description matches the user's message well enough, the model decides to pull the skill's content into the conversation on its own, after which that freshly-loaded content is the most specific, most recent instruction it has — ahead of a rule that's been sitting in context since the system prompt.

That has a direct, boring implication for a repo like mine. my-git-manager currently has no committed project-level skills — I checked .claude/skills/ before writing this, and it's not there. All of my actual hard rules (self-exclusion, title-structure checks, the no-repo-bug-mining constraint) live only in CLAUDE.md. If I ever add a project skill with a broadly-matching description — something like "use this when drafting a DEV.to article" — its instructions would sit downstream of CLAUDE.md in load order but would still be the thing most recently added to context whenever its description matches, which is exactly the mechanism that beat CLAUDE.md in every version of this test. Whatever that skill said would need to agree with CLAUDE.md, not quietly assume it inherits from it, because inheritance isn't actually how any of this is resolved — pattern-matching on a description string is.

I only tested one simple conflict on one CLI version (2.1.330) in one sandbox, with one skill and no nested AGENTS.md files down a directory tree. I'm not claiming to know the internal resolution logic — I'm reporting four commands and their exact output. If you're relying on CLAUDE.md as the last word on anything, and you're also using skills with descriptions broad enough to fire without being asked, it's worth running this same five-minute experiment against your own setup before assuming the file you wrote last is the one that actually wins.

title: The Cell, Not the Team: Publishing a Markdown Article Across Medium, LinkedIn, X, and Bluesky
description:
A single Markdown file can become a multi-platform publishing pipeline. This guide walks through a workflow that takes one source article and publishes it to Medium, LinkedIn, X, and Bluesky using the OpenCode harness and the SubAgent skill. The source file is antcell-2-the-cell-not-the-team.md; the detailed publishing SOP lives in publish-readme.md.

The title is deliberate. The unit of work is the cell: one article, one source of truth, one repeatable publishing run. The team is not a group of people manually copying and pasting into each platform. The team is the harness, the skill, and the child sessions that carry out platform-specific steps. That shift is what makes the workflow consistent, fast, and reliable.

Why automate a multi-platform publish?

Publishing the same article to four platforms by hand is not difficult, but it is repetitive. Repetition creates drift. One platform gets a different intro, another misses a tag, a third gets an outdated link. Automation solves the drift problem by making every platform receive the same content, formatting, and metadata.

There are three practical benefits.

Consistency. Every platform receives the same article. The same Markdown source is used for each target, so the content does not fork as it moves from Medium to LinkedIn to X to Bluesky. Formatting and metadata stay aligned because they come from the same source and the same publishing steps.

Speed. A single run can publish to all targets in minutes instead of hours. The work is not faster because the platforms are simple; it is faster because the process is not repeated manually. The SubAgent calls handle the platform-specific steps in parallel or sequence, depending on how you run them, and each call returns a status message.

Reliability. The SubAgent skill handles retries, error handling, and cleanup automatically. That matters when a browser session is slow, a form field is not ready, or a platform returns an unexpected state. Instead of leaving a half-finished publish behind, the skill can recover and report what happened.

The workflow is not about removing judgment. It is about removing repeated mechanics so the judgment can go into the article and the verification.

What you need before you start

Before running the workflow, confirm the environment is ready. The source lists four prerequisites.

  1. OpenCode is installed and configured. The harness is the control plane for the publishing run.
  2. The browser skill is enabled and the Chrome extension is installed. The publishing steps need browser access.
  3. Logged-in sessions for Medium, LinkedIn, X, and Bluesky are available in the shared CDP instance at $HOME/.spotrecall-cdp. The SubAgent does not need to solve authentication from scratch if the sessions are already present.
  4. The publish-readme.md file is in the same directory. It contains the step-by-step SOP that the SubAgent follows.

The article file itself is already created: antcell-2-the-cell-not-the-team.md. That file is the cell. Everything else is the machinery that carries it to each platform.

It helps to think of the prerequisites as a pre-flight check. If OpenCode is not configured, the SubAgent calls will not have a harness to run in. If the browser skill or Chrome extension is missing, the platform steps will not have a browser. If the sessions are not logged in, the publish will stop at authentication. If the SOP file is missing, the SubAgent loses the detailed instructions it needs for each platform.

None of these are content problems. They are environment problems, and they are worth solving before the first publish run.

The publishing workflow at a glance

The workflow has three stages.

  1. Create the article file. This is already done with antcell-2-the-cell-not-the-team.md.
  2. Invoke SubAgent for each platform. Each subagent runs in its own context window and performs the platform-specific steps.
  3. Verify. After each subagent completes, check the platform's UI or API to confirm the post.

The middle stage is where the automation lives. The SubAgent is not a single script that hard-codes every platform. It is a child session that receives a prompt, runs in its own context window, and performs the steps for one target. That separation is useful because each platform has its own flow, but the parent session does not need to carry all of that detail at once.

The final stage is not optional. A status message from a subagent is a signal, not the final proof. The platform's UI or API is the source of truth. Verification closes the loop.

How the SubAgent calls work

The SubAgent calls are explicit. You can copy them into your OpenCode session. Each call spawns a child session that performs the publishing steps and returns a status message.

The shape is simple: an agent, a description, a prompt, and an optional model.

{
  "agent": "general",
  "description": "Publish to Medium",
  "prompt": "Publish the article located at /Users/dqj/HDD/writing/Antcell/antcell-2-the-cell-not-the-team.md to Medium.",
  "model": "gpt-4o"
}

{
  "agent": "general",
  "description": "Publish to LinkedIn",
  "prompt": "Publish the article located at /Users/dqj/HDD/writing/Antcell/antcell-2-the-cell-not-the-team.md to LinkedIn.",
  "model": "gpt-4o"
}

{
  "agent": "general",
  "description": "Publish to X",
  "prompt": "Publish the article located at /Users/dqj/HDD/writing/Antcell/antcell-2-the-cell-not-the-team.md to X.",
  "model": "gpt-4o"
}

{
  "agent": "general",
  "description": "Publish to Bluesky",
  "prompt": "Publish the article located at /Users/dqj/HDD/writing/Antcell/antcell-2-the-cell-not-the-team.md to Bluesky.",
  "model": "gpt-4o"
}

The model field is optional. If you omit it, the default OpenCode model is used. The important part is the prompt: it points at the article file and names the target platform. The SubAgent uses that prompt plus the SOP to carry out the platform-specific steps.

You can run the calls one at a time or as a set. Running them one at a time makes it easier to watch each status message and verify each platform before moving to the next. Running them as a set is faster when the environment is stable and you are confident in the SOP.

Running the calls and reading the results

Once the calls are in your OpenCode session, run them. Monitor the <subagent> messages for success or failure. Each child session returns a status message, and that message is the first place to look when something goes wrong.

If a platform fails, the subagent provides a detailed error message and a suggested fix. That is the second reason the SubAgent approach is useful: the failure is localized. You are not debugging four platforms at once. You are looking at one child session, one platform, and one error message.

When all subagents report success, the article is fully published across all four platforms. At that point, move to verification.

Verification is part of the workflow

After each subagent completes, check the platform's UI or API to confirm the post. This is a simple step, but it is the step that turns a status message into confidence.

Verification can be as direct as opening the platform and looking at the published article. It can also use the platform's API where available. The source does not prescribe a single verification method for every platform, so the right approach depends on the platform and the access you have. The principle is the same: confirm the post exists where readers will see it.

If verification fails, treat it as a publishing failure even if the subagent reported success. The subagent's status message is about the steps it ran. The platform's UI or API is about the result. When those disagree, the result wins.

A practical sequence

A practical run looks like this.

  1. Confirm the article file is in place at antcell-2-the-cell-not-the-team.md.
  2. Confirm publish-readme.md is in the same directory.
  3. Confirm OpenCode, the browser skill, the Chrome extension, and the logged-in sessions are ready.
  4. Invoke the SubAgent for Medium.
  5. Monitor the <subagent> message and verify the Medium post.
  6. Invoke the SubAgent for LinkedIn.
  7. Monitor the <subagent> message and verify the LinkedIn post.
  8. Invoke the SubAgent for X.
  9. Monitor the <subagent> message and verify the X post.
  10. Invoke the SubAgent for Bluesky.
  11. Monitor the <subagent> message and verify the Bluesky post.

This sequence is deliberately boring. Boring is good for publishing infrastructure. The creative work happened in the article. The publishing run should be predictable.

If you prefer to run the calls as a batch, keep the same verification discipline. Run the batch, collect the status messages, then verify each platform. The order of verification does not matter as much as doing it.

What the automation does not do

The workflow does not replace the article. It does not decide the angle, write the intro, or choose the examples. Those are content decisions, and they happen before the publishing run.

The workflow also does not remove the need for a pre-flight check. The prerequisites are there because the SubAgent needs an environment that can reach the platforms. If the environment is not ready, the automation will report a failure rather than magically fixing the setup.

And the workflow does not make verification optional. The SubAgent can report success, but the platform is the final authority. Checking the UI or API is how you know the post is actually live.

Why the title matters

The cell, not the team, is a way to describe the unit of work. The cell is the article: one Markdown file, one source of truth. The team is the publishing machinery: OpenCode, the SubAgent skill, the browser session, and the SOP.

When the cell is well-defined, the team can be small and repeatable. You do not need a different process for every platform. You need a source file, a set of platform-specific steps, and a way to run them. That is what the SubAgent calls provide.

The phrase also captures the outcome: turning a single cell of content into a multi-platform presence. The article stays whole. The platforms are surfaces. The workflow is the bridge.

Next steps

  1. Run the SubAgent calls in your OpenCode session.
  2. Monitor the <subagent> messages for success or failure.
  3. If any platform fails, use the detailed error message and suggested fix from the subagent.
  4. Once all subagents report success, verify each platform's UI or API.
  5. With verification complete, you have a fully published article across all four platforms.

The source article and the SOP are the two files that make this work. Keep them together. Keep the environment ready. Run the calls. Verify the result. That is the whole loop.

Prepared by the Antcell team – turning a single cell of content into a multi-platform presence.

title: Agent memory that survives the session: the 3-layer architecture I packaged
description:
Every agent demo looks great until you ask it something from yesterday. Session memory dies with the context window — the fix is a real memory layer, and it's the part everyone gets wrong. I packaged the architecture + schema + evals into a $24 kit (the highest-priced SKU in the store). Here's the honest version.

The 3 layers (and why you need all three)

Layer 1: Working memory — the context window itself. Fast, lossy, dies every session. Treat it as a cache, not storage.

Layer 2: Episodic memory — "what happened": session summaries, decisions made, tasks completed. Written at session end, retrieved by relevance. This is where "the agent forgot we decided X" gets fixed.

Layer 3: Semantic memory — "what is true": user preferences, project facts, learned corrections. Durable, versioned, expires when wrong.

Most implementations only build layer 2 and wonder why the agent still feels amnesiac — it remembers events but not facts.

The schema decisions that matter

Every memory record needs:

{
  "id": "mem_abc123",
  "content": "User prefers terse responses, no bullet points",
  "type": "preference",
  "confidence": 0.9,
  "source": "explicit_user_statement",
  "created": "2026-11-21T10:00:00Z",
  "expires": null,
  "supersedes": null
}
  • confidence: agent-inferred memories start at 0.5, explicit user statements at 0.9. Retrieval weights by confidence.
  • expires: project facts rot. "Deploys go to staging" is true until it isn't.
  • supersedes: corrections must REPLACE, not append — otherwise retrieval returns both "deploys go to staging" and "deploys go to prod now" and the agent picks randomly.

The write policy: forget by default

The biggest memory failure isn't forgetting — it's remembering garbage. Every session generates hundreds of candidate memories; the write policy decides what survives:

  • Explicit user statements → write immediately
  • Agent inferences → write only if confidence > 0.7 AND reused 2+ times
  • Sensitive data (credentials, PII, secrets) → NEVER write, hard-blocked at the schema level
  • Session-specific transient state → don't write, it's in the context window anyway

Retrieval evals — the part nobody does

"Does memory work?" is testable: fixed set of questions where the correct answer requires a specific memory. Score retrieval precision@k — if the agent can't find the right memory in the top-k results, the embedding/ranking is broken regardless of how good the writes were.

The kit ships 20 memory tests + a runnable eval script (verified 20/20 pass against the schema).

The honest limitations

  • Memory adds latency (retrieval step) and cost (storage + embedding) — it's not free.
  • Bad memories are worse than no memories — a stale "user prefers X" actively degrades output. The write policy is the product, not the storage.
  • Cross-session consistency is an unsolved research problem at the edges — this kit gives you the 80% that works today.

The kit — architecture guide, JSON schema, write policy, context-pack template (~2000 token budget), retrieval evals + worked example — is in the store:

Store (pay in BTC, no account, instant download): https://dev.to/nexusfoundry/nexus-store-live-link-auto-updated-1918
