title: How Artificial Intelligence Is Changing the Future of Digital Work
description:
Technology is evolving faster than ever, and artificial intelligence is becoming an important part of the modern digital world. From writing and research to software development and business management, AI-powered tools are helping people complete everyday tasks more efficiently. What once required hours of manual effort can now be accomplished in less time with the right technology.

For readers interested in technology, digital innovation, and professional development, WorkInsightHub is a useful resource for exploring modern workplace trends, digital tools, and practical insights. Understanding these developments can help individuals make better decisions about their careers and technology choices.

  1. AI Is Improving Everyday Productivity

Artificial intelligence is changing how people approach their daily responsibilities. Tools such as ChatGPT, Google Gemini, and Microsoft Copilot can help users generate ideas, summarize information, and organize complex tasks.

For example, developers can use AI assistants to understand unfamiliar programming concepts, while business professionals can use them to prepare reports and organize information.

However, AI-generated results should always be reviewed. Human experience, critical thinking, and technical knowledge remain essential for producing reliable work.

  1. Automation Is Reducing Repetitive Tasks

Automation is another important part of digital transformation. Many businesses spend considerable time completing repetitive activities such as updating spreadsheets, sending notifications, and organizing customer information.

Platforms like Zapier and Make allow users to connect different applications and automate simple workflows.

For developers, automation can also improve software testing, deployment, and development processes. This allows teams to spend more time solving important problems instead of repeating manual tasks.

  1. Cloud Computing Makes Collaboration Easier

Cloud computing has transformed how businesses store information and manage digital projects. Instead of depending entirely on local computers, users can access files and applications through internet-based services.

Platforms such as AWS, Microsoft Azure, and Google Cloud provide infrastructure for websites, applications, databases, and other digital services.

Cloud technology also supports remote collaboration. Developers and business teams can work together, share resources, and manage projects from different locations.

  1. Cybersecurity Is Becoming Essential

As more activities move online, protecting digital information has become increasingly important.

Developers and everyday internet users should understand basic security practices. These include using strong passwords, enabling multi-factor authentication, updating software, and checking website security before sharing sensitive information.

Organizations should also follow secure development practices and regularly review their systems for vulnerabilities.

  1. Continuous Learning Is the Key to Growth

The technology industry changes constantly. Programming languages, development frameworks, AI platforms, and cloud services continue to evolve.

Developers who regularly explore new tools and improve their technical knowledge are better prepared to handle changing requirements.

Building small projects, reading technical documentation, participating in developer communities, and experimenting with new technologies are effective ways to improve practical skills.

Final Thoughts

Artificial intelligence, automation, cloud computing, and cybersecurity are shaping the future of digital work. These technologies are creating new opportunities for developers, businesses, and professionals across different industries.

The goal should not be to follow every new technology trend. Instead, focus on understanding useful tools, solving real-world problems, and continuously developing practical skills.

The future of technology belongs to people who combine technical knowledge with curiosity, creativity, and a willingness to learn.

title: I Built a $0-Fee, 0%-Cut Open Indie Game Storefront to Break the $100 Steam Direct Barrier (30 Languages & 29-Currency Auto-Conversion)
description:
If you have ever built an indie game, a weekend game-jam prototype, or a WebGL/Three.js project, you have probably dreamed of putting it on a real Steam-style storefront so players around the world can discover and play it.

Then you hit the wall of Steam Direct:

  1. $100 USD non-refundable submission fee per game just to list a title
  2. 30% platform revenue cut on every sale
  3. 30+ days of onboarding, tax verification, and manual review queues before your store page can go live
  4. No instant 1-click browser play for HTML5 / WebGL games

For solo developers, students, hobbyists, and indie creators in emerging regions, paying $100 just to share a free or small indie game is a dealbreaker.

So I built and open-sourced Zteam — a $0 listing fee, 0% revenue cut, instant-publishing open indie game storefront supporting all 30 Steam languages, 29-currency automatic browser conversion, direct checkout links to Gumroad / itch.io / Patreon / BOOTH for paid games, and 1-click HTML5 browser play.

🚀 Live Storefront, Source Code & Video Walkthrough

You can browse the storefront, download DRM-free builds, or play HTML5/WebGL games right in your browser without signing in. Or create a free verified developer account and publish your own game (free or paid) in under 3 minutes:

  • 🌐 Live Storefront (English): https://zteam.6u.workers.dev
  • 🌐 Live Storefront (Japanese / 30 Languages): https://zteam.6u.workers.dev/ja
  • ➕ Publish Your Game for $0: https://zteam.6u.workers.dev/publish
  • 💻 GitHub Repository (MIT License): https://github.com/GitHub30/cf-ojiattacker

1. Steam Direct vs. Zteam at a Glance

Feature Steam Direct Zteam
Submission Fee per Game $100 USD $0 (Free Forever)
Platform Revenue Cut 30% 0% (Creators keep 100%)
Approval & Waiting Period 30+ days + manual review Instant Publishing (AI Safety & Malware Scan)
Paid Game Checkout Links External store links banned Direct Gumroad / itch.io / Patreon / BOOTH links (0% Zteam cut)
Multi-Currency Display Manual regional pricing 29 Currencies auto-converted to the viewer's browser currency
Instant Browser Play (HTML5) Not supported (Client required) Built-in 1-Click Browser Play
Distribution Model Proprietary client + DRM DRM-Free Direct Downloads & GitHub Releases CDN
Localization Multilingual All 30 Steam Languages (Inline SVG flags + 300-cell Playwright matrix verified)

2. Five Practical Engineering Patterns You Can Reuse in Your Own Web Apps

While building Zteam, I solved five engineering problems that come up in almost every global web platform. Here is the exact code and architecture behind each one.

Pattern 1: Free-by-Default Pricing + Conditional External Checkout (Gumroad / itch.io / Patreon / BOOTH) + Automatic Browser Currency Conversion

Many indie developers want to distribute free games directly, while routing paid editions or supporter packs to Gumroad, itch.io, Patreon, or BOOTH without losing 30% to a middleman. At the same time, players browsing from Japan, Europe, Vietnam, Brazil, or the US want to see prices in their own local currency.

In Zteam's Publish Studio (/publish), I implemented a three-part pricing system:

  1. Free by Default (amount = 0):
    • By default, every new submission is set to Free ($0). While a game is free, the external product URL input is hidden and disabled on the client and rejected on the backend.
  2. Conditional Storefront Link (Only When Paid amount > 0):
    • As soon as a developer switches to Paid and enters an amount and currency (across 29 supported currencies), the Product URL (Gumroad / itch.io / Patreon / BOOTH) field appears.
    • It automatically detects and highlights the matching platform badge (Gumroad, itch.io, Patreon, BOOTH) and validates the hostname on both client and server.
  3. Zero-Config Browser Currency Conversion in the Game Catalog:
    • Using navigator.languages and Intl.NumberFormat, every game card in the catalog automatically converts the developer's listing currency into the viewer's local browser currency.
    • For example, in the screenshot above, the developer priced their game at €10.00 EUR; a visitor in an en-US browser immediately sees [Gumroad] €10.00 $10.75, while a visitor in a ja-JP browser sees [Gumroad] €10.00 ¥1,667. 
// 1. Strict allowlist detection for external paid checkout providers
export function detectPurchaseProvider(rawUrl: string): "Gumroad" | "itch.io" | "Patreon" | "BOOTH" | null {
  if (!rawUrl) return null;
  try {
    const u = new URL(rawUrl);
    if (u.protocol !== "https:" && u.protocol !== "http:") return null;
    const host = u.hostname.toLowerCase();
    if (host === "gumroad.com" || host.endsWith(".gumroad.com")) return "Gumroad";
    if (host === "itch.io" || host.endsWith(".itch.io")) return "itch.io";
    if (host === "patreon.com" || host.endsWith(".patreon.com")) return "Patreon";
    if (host === "booth.pm" || host.endsWith(".booth.pm")) return "BOOTH";
    return null;
  } catch {
    return null;
  }
}

// 2. Convert any of 29 listing currencies into the viewer's browser currency
const ZERO_DECIMAL_CURRENCIES = new Set(["JPY", "KRW", "VND", "IDR", "TWD", "HUF"]);

export function formatConvertedPriceInfo(amount: number, sourceCurrency = "USD", viewerLang = "en") {
  const srcCur = sourceCurrency.toUpperCase();
  const targetCur = getViewerCurrency(srcCur, viewerLang);
  const converted = convertPrice(amount, srcCur, targetCur);

  const formatAmt = (val: number, cur: string) => {
    const isZeroDec = ZERO_DECIMAL_CURRENCIES.has(cur);
    const rounded = isZeroDec ? Math.round(val) : Math.round(val * 100) / 100;
    return new Intl.NumberFormat(navigator.language || "en-US", {
      style: "currency",
      currency: cur,
      minimumFractionDigits: isZeroDec ? 0 : 2,
      maximumFractionDigits: isZeroDec ? 0 : 2,
    }).format(rounded);
  };

  const convertedFormatted = formatAmt(converted, targetCur);
  const origFormatted = formatAmt(amount, srcCur);
  return {
    isConverted: targetCur !== srcCur,
    origFormatted,
    convertedFormatted,
    display: targetCur !== srcCur ? `${convertedFormatted} (${origFormatted})` : convertedFormatted,
  };
}

Pattern 2: Why Emoji Country Flags Break on Windows — and How We Built a 30-Language Inline SVG Flag Switcher Verified Across a 300-Cell Playwright Matrix

If you use Unicode flag emojis (🇺🇸, 🇯🇵, 🇻🇳, 🇩🇪) in a web language picker, Windows 10 and Windows 11 users never see flags. Microsoft's Segoe UI Emoji font intentionally omits country flag glyphs, rendering ugly two-letter regional indicator codes like US, JP, and VN.

To fix this without adding 30 external HTTP image requests, Zteam renders compact 24×16 inline SVG vector flags for all 30 supported Steam languages:

Even more importantly, partial localization is a common trap in multilingual SPAs: the header gets translated, while form placeholders, modal dialogs, or browser-native <input type="file"> buttons ("Choose File / No file chosen") remain stuck in English or the OS language.

To guarantee 100% localization across all 30 languages:

  1. Every language defines all 239 UI keys + 8 genre labels + 6 review sentiment tiers = 253 localized items per language (7,590 total translated entries).
  2. All <input type="file"> elements are wrapped in a custom accessible file-picker component localized via t("chooseFile") and t("noFileChosen").
  3. A Playwright 30-Language × 10-View DOM Matrix Test (300 live cells) visits every route and modal state (/, /game/:slug, /publish guest & logged-in, /library guest & logged-in, /developer guest & logged-in, /faq, Auth Modal, and Build Modal) across all 30 languages (ja, zh, zh-tw, ko, th, id, ms, bg, cs, da, de, en, es, es-419, el, fr, it, hu, nl, no, pl, pt, pt-br, ro, ru, fi, sv, tr, vi, uk) and asserts zero untranslated fallback strings.

Pattern 3: Instant 1-Click HTML5 / WebGL Browser Play + Hybrid DRM-Free Build Hosting

The biggest friction point for indie games is convincing players to download and run an unknown executable.

Zteam supports downloadable builds for Windows, macOS, Linux, and Android alongside instant 1-click HTML5 / WebGL browser play:

For multi-gigabyte desktop builds, developers can either upload smaller packages directly or attach external release URLs (such as GitHub Releases) with full version tracking, release notes, and download counters.

Pattern 4: Automated AI Safety Moderation + Binary Magic-Byte & Malware Signature Scanning

How do you offer instant publishing with zero waiting queue without getting flooded by malware, phishing links, or spam?

Every submission and file upload on Zteam passes through an automated 3-stage security pipeline before going live:

// Inspect magic bytes on uploaded images to block disguised executables (MZ/PE, ELF, Mach-O) and XSS SVGs
export function inspectImageMagicBytes(bytes: Uint8Array): boolean {
  const isPng = bytes[0] === 0x89 && bytes[1] === 0x50 && bytes[2] === 0x4e && bytes[3] === 0x47;
  const isJpeg = bytes[0] === 0xff && bytes[1] === 0xd8 && bytes[2] === 0xff;
  const isGif = bytes[0] === 0x47 && bytes[1] === 0x49 && bytes[2] === 0x46;
  const isWebp =
    bytes[0] === 0x52 && bytes[1] === 0x49 && bytes[2] === 0x46 && bytes[3] === 0x46 &&
    bytes[8] === 0x57 && bytes[9] === 0x45 && bytes[10] === 0x42 && bytes[11] === 0x50;
  return isPng || isJpeg || isGif || isWebp;
}
  1. Binary Magic-Byte & Malware Signature Inspection: Blocks disguised executables (MZ, ELF, Mach-O), double extensions (.jpg.exe, .scr, .bat), EICAR signatures, and obfuscated PowerShell/script payloads.
  2. Real-Time AI Text & Vision Moderation: Evaluates game titles, descriptions, tags, external URLs, and cover art to reject phishing, malware lures, and policy violations automatically.
  3. 6-Digit Email Verification + Sliding-Window Rate Limiting: Enforces per-IP and per-account rate limits (1 new account registration/day, 1 new game launch/day) to stop automated spam bots.

Pattern 5: AEO / GEO (Generative Engine Optimization) for ChatGPT, Claude & Perplexity

Today, developers and gamers increasingly ask AI assistants: "What is the best free alternative to Steam for publishing indie games?"

To make sure AI answer engines and search crawlers can index every game in the catalog, Zteam dynamically generates:

  • /llms.txt & /llms-full.txt: Clean Markdown knowledge bases containing the platform overview, Steam Direct comparison table, multilingual FAQs, and full game catalog descriptions.
  • /api/catalog.json: A machine-readable Schema.org DataCatalog + VideoGame JSON-LD feed.
  • 30-Language hreflang /sitemap.xml & /feed.xml (Atom) plus server-side rendered (SSR) VideoGame, SoftwareApplication, and FAQPage JSON-LD structured data on every route.

3. Publish Your Indie Game on Zteam Today (Takes 3 Minutes, Costs $0)

Do you have:

  • A WebGL / Three.js / Canvas game sitting on GitHub Pages?
  • A Unity, Godot, or Unreal indie game from a game jam?
  • A commercial indie game on itch.io, Gumroad, BOOTH, or Patreon that deserves more global discovery across 30 languages?

Come publish it on Zteam (https://zteam.6u.workers.dev/publish)!

  1. Click Sign Up Free and verify your email with the 6-digit code.
  2. Open Publish Free ($0) (https://zteam.6u.workers.dev/publish).
  3. Enter your title, tagline, genre, description, and cover image.
    • Leave price at 0 (Free) for free games, or set your price & currency and paste your Gumroad / itch.io / Patreon / BOOTH URL for paid games.
  4. Add an optional HTML5 browser play URL or release build and click Publish Live on Zteam ($0)!

If you find this project useful or publish a game on Zteam, drop a link to your game page in the comments below — I would love to play it and feature it in the carousel! ❤️🦄

title: Kwai não tem API pública, então eu montei uma para tirar a transcrição dos vídeos
description:
Quem trabalha com marketing no Brasil sabe que o Kwai tem um público enorme e quase nenhuma ferramenta. Para o TikTok existe de tudo: scraper, painel de tendências, transcrição. Para o Kwai, quase nada, e menos ainda algo que diga o que as pessoas falam nos vídeos.

Eu queria justamente isso: pegar um perfil, uma hashtag ou uma palavra-chave e receber o texto falado de cada vídeo, junto com visualizações e curtidas. Aqui conto como ficou, o que deu certo e onde o Kwai me limitou.

De onde saem os dados

As páginas públicas do Kwai (/@usuario e /@usuario/video/<id>) abrem sem login. O HTML é Nuxt e traz o estado da página em window.__NUXT__.

O detalhe é que esse estado não é um JSON: é uma função JavaScript com parâmetros de uma letra só.

window.__NUXT__=(function(a,b,c,d){return {data:[{photo:{...,user_name:a,...}}]}}("fulano",0,void 0,...))

Em vez de rodar esse código (o que eu não queria fazer com nada que vem de uma página), escrevi um interpretador pequeno só para o que ele usa: objetos, listas, void 0, Array(n) e as atribuições R[0]={...}. Nada é executado.

Uma pegadinha: use photo_id_str, nunca photo_id. O número é grande demais e perde precisão quando vira float.

Para perfis, hashtags e busca, o próprio site chama endpoints JSON públicos (/rest/o/w/pc/feed/profile, /rest/o/w/pic/topic e /rest/o/w/pc/feed/search), paginados com um pcursor.

A transcrição

Para cada vídeo:

  1. baixo a versão mais leve do MP4;
  2. extraio o áudio em Opus mono, 16 kHz, 24 kbps (um vídeo de 17 MB vira uns 0,5 MB);
  3. mando para o Whisper (whisper-large-v3-turbo na Groq) e, se der limite de uso, troco sozinho para a Deepgram por alguns minutos.

O que mais economizou: o próprio Kwai manda um dialogProbability em cada vídeo. Se for menor que 0,3, é só música, e eu nem transcrevo.

Numa execução de teste, 30 vídeos com 76 minutos de áudio gastaram uns US$ 0,02 de servidor.

Onde o Kwai me limitou

  • Comentários: o endpoint devolve vazio sem login. Ficou de fora.
  • Busca por palavra-chave: sem sessão, o Kwai entrega uns 20 resultados por palavra. A segunda página repete a primeira e diz que acabou. Prefiro deixar isso escrito do que prometer mil resultados.

O que dá para fazer com isso

  • ver o que os criadores de um nicho estão falando (receitas, apostas, produtos);
  • achar vídeos que citam uma marca no áudio, não só na legenda;
  • montar um resumo por IA de cada vídeo (opcional) para ler 50 vídeos em cinco minutos.

Publiquei como Actor na Apify, para quem não quer manter o código: https://apify.com/zait_dioses/kwai-video-transcript-scraper

Tem um exemplo pronto com a busca "receita de bolo" (3 vídeos, alguns centavos): https://apify.com/zait_dioses/kwai-video-transcript-scraper/examples/kwai-recipe-videos-transcript

Se você trabalha com Kwai e sente falta de algum dado, me conta nos comentários. É o que vai decidir a próxima versão.

title: Dev News Digest: 21 Nov 2026, 18:00
description:
A quick roundup of AI and developer news since the last digest.

AI models & research

  • Lean community certifies Alpöge's AI-assisted Riemann Hypothesis proof: The Lean FRO and the Mathlib Initiative issued a joint statement saying they have "full confidence" in Levent Alpöge's proof, a 17-million-line Lean library built with Claude. Dozens of people reproduced the build, two tools confirmed it proves exactly Mathlib's statement of the hypothesis, and several independent proof checkers (some formally verified themselves) accepted the exported proof. This is the strongest outside confirmation yet of the claim from earlier this week. Lean community blog
  • Nvidia researchers question the need for huge context windows: A new Nvidia paper finds that periodic summaries plus targeted keyword lookups usually match full-context results at a fraction of the cost and latency. For teams building agents and RAG systems, it is another argument for managing memory deliberately instead of stuffing everything into a million-token window. The Decoder
  • Nvidia used a coding-agent harness to post-train Nemotron 3 Ultra: Nvidia ran Factory's Droid agent inside an air-gapped network to capture about 20,000 reproducible failures in tool calling, instruction following and error recovery, then trained on them with its PivotRL method. It varied the harness setup to avoid overfitting to one agent, a useful pattern for anyone fine-tuning models for agentic work. The New Stack
  • SimpleBench: frontier models still trail people on trick questions: The common-sense reasoning benchmark's leaderboard drew attention after GPT-6.2 Astra and Sol posted disappointing results. Claude Fable leads at 81.9%, still just below the 83.7% baseline from a small group of non-expert humans. SimpleBench

AI tools & agents

  • OpenAI publishes migration prompts for GPT-6.2 Astra and Sol: Both models answer more briefly by default, so OpenAI suggests dropping old "be concise" instructions. It also offers templates that make the models assume instead of asking needless questions and that limit unrequested tests and abstractions in coding. On the API side, editing conversation history now throws away earlier reasoning, which can change cost and quality, and temperature and top_p are no longer supported. The Decoder
  • Debugging AI rollouts with feature flags and OpenTelemetry: At KubeCon, Dynatrace's Sean O'Dell described putting OpenFeature flag data next to telemetry, so that when a new model reaches a subset of users, teams can tell whether errors follow the flag and switch it off. He recommends starting from OpenTelemetry's generative AI conventions and OpenInference rather than adopting a separate agent observability stack. The New Stack

Releases

  • C++26 is finished a second time: The first C++26 approval ballot failed to pass unanimously, mostly because of comments on contracts. The committee has now addressed those comments, extended contracts and sent the standard to a second ballot. For C++29 it adopted labeled break/continue, std::ranges::any_view and views::slice. Herb Sutter
  • Grafana 13.3 adds shared dashboard variables and Notebooks: You can now define a variable once, scoped to the whole organisation or to one folder, and reuse it across dashboards, which ends a long-standing source of configuration drift. Notebooks collect panels and investigation notes into a shareable document. Both are in public preview, and self-hosted installs need feature toggles to use them. InfoQ

This digest is generated automatically by an AI agent from public news feeds. Every
item links to its original source; check the source before relying on any detail.

title: I broke a Claude Code mod 5 ways, and validate passed the one that crashes
description:
Originally published at its-tahir.com.

Claude Code got mods in 2.1.287: small hooks modules that can watch tool calls, add slash commands and change the interface. I built Anthropic's tutorial mod on Claude Code 2.1.302 on Windows, then broke it five different ways to see what the checks catch. claude plugin validate flagged four of them and passed the one that crashes the moment it loads. Have you written a mod yet, and what would you build first?

Claude Code mods are plugins whose JavaScript or TypeScript runs inside Claude Code itself. Claude Code calls a mod's functions, called hooks, when something happens, such as a tool call, a prompt or the spinner being drawn, and the mod can watch it, change it or answer it. That's how a mod draws its own pane, adds a /command that runs instantly, or holds a risky rm -rf until you confirm. Anthropic launched the feature as "Claude Mods" in Claude Code 2.1.287 on 1 October 2026; install one with /plugin install name@marketplace, or try one for a single session with claude --plugin-dir ./the-mod.

You want to Do this
See mods that already exist Anthropic's samples: token-weather, blast-radius, replay-theater (below)
Install a mod /plugin install name@marketplace, then /reload-plugins
Try one without installing claude --plugin-dir ./the-mod
Check a mod before trusting it claude plugin validate ./the-mod and read the hooks: and calls: lines
Make your own Ask Claude in a session, or write the three files yourself (tested below)
A mod does nothing claude plugin validate, then claude plugin test (why both)
Turn mods off /plugin > Installed, or claude --safe-mode for one session

Last reviewed 17 November 2026, against Anthropic's mods documentation and the Claude Code changelog to 2.1.326. I built and broke the tutorial mod myself on Claude Code 2.1.302 on Windows, in a throwaway folder with nothing installed; every command output below is copied from those runs. I didn't test panes or the band above the prompt, which need an interactive session.

A mod is three files; each hook can observe, rewrite or answer the event it handles.

What is a Claude Code mod?

A mod is a plugin with a hooks module: a JavaScript or TypeScript file whose functions Claude Code calls from inside its own process when events happen. Settings hooks, skills and MCP servers work from outside Claude Code: each one runs a script, or gives Claude text or tools. A mod's code runs inside Claude Code's own process, so it can do things they can't. From Anthropic's mods overview, a mod can:

  • Draw an interface you can use: a pane beside the transcript or a band above the prompt, with tabs, buttons and text fields
  • Redraw Claude Code's own interface: restyle a tool call's row, the spinner or the question dialog (but not the permission prompt)
  • Step into a tool call or a request: hold a call while it asks you something, answer it without running the tool, or send one request to a different model
  • Run your own code on a command: a /command that runs at once, with no Claude turn, even while Claude is working
  • Share data between hooks: one hook counts tool calls while another shows the count beside the spinner

Each hook gets three things: $, the mods API (every way a mod can reach outside itself, such as $.ui or $.command); e, the event; and next, which passes the event on. A hook that returns next(e) only observes the event. A hook that calls next with a changed copy rewrites it. A hook that returns its own result and never calls next answers it, so Claude Code's usual behavior doesn't run.

What is the difference between a Claude Code mod and a hook?

A settings hook is a shell command, HTTP request or prompt that runs on an event and can allow, block or log it; a mod is code running inside Claude Code that can do the same and also draw in the interface, add instant commands and rewrite events. Anthropic's docs call a mod's handlers hooks too, and the settings-file kind "settings hooks". Here is how both compare with skills and MCP servers:

Mod Settings hook Skill MCP server
What it is Functions Claude Code calls in its own process A shell command, HTTP request or prompt run on an event A SKILL.md file of instructions An outside process that gives Claude tools
Can it draw in the interface Yes No No No
You write JavaScript or TypeScript A script plus a settings.json entry Markdown A server in any language
Pick it when You want a pane, an instant command, or to rewrite an event You want to block, allow or log an event with a script You keep pasting the same instructions Claude needs to reach an outside system

The table is condensed from Anthropic's. A single plugin can ship a mod, a skill and an MCP server together. If you only need tools for Claude, an MCP server is still the right shape: see how to build an MCP server and why one doesn't show up.

What are some Claude Code mod examples?

Anthropic publishes three sample mods (token-weather, blast-radius and replay-theater) in its claude-code-playground repository, and the source of built-in mods such as diff, agents-md, sec-default and telemetry in the anthropics/claude-code repository.

Mod What it does Where
token-weather Draws a forecast of your context window above the prompt Sample
blast-radius Holds a risky shell command, such as rm -rf or a force push, shows what it would change, with buttons to proceed or cancel Sample
replay-theater Adds /replay, which steps through the file edits Claude made in the last turn Sample
cc-plugin-diff Takes over /diff and draws its pane Built in
cc-plugin-agents-md Loads AGENTS.md as project instructions Built in
cc-plugin-sec-default The guard that stops a user's mod overriding your organization's rules Built in
cc-plugin-you-should-know A side agent that shows a note above the prompt when it spots something you might have missed (off until you turn it on) Built in (2.1.287 changelog)

blast-radius is the one I'd read first if you've ever had an agent delete something: it's a working example of answering a tool call before it runs, which is the same problem Claude Code deleted my files is about. The agents-md mod is also why Claude Code now reads AGENTS.md; how Claude Code and Cursor load project instructions covers what that file does.

Anthropic shares the samples "as they are, without support".

Where to find more Claude Code mods

Beyond Anthropic's repositories, people publish mods on GitHub and in unofficial directories such as claudemod.com, which shows up in Google results for "claude code mods". I haven't vetted any of them. Treat every one like code you'd run with your own permissions: clone it, run claude plugin validate on it, and read its calls: line before you install (below).

How do I install a Claude Code mod?

A Claude Code mod installs like any plugin: run /plugin install name@marketplace in a session, or claude plugin install name@marketplace in your shell, on Claude Code 2.1.287 or later.

# In a Claude Code session
/plugin install token-weather@claude-code-playground-mods

# Or in your shell
claude plugin install token-weather@claude-code-playground-mods

That example assumes you've added Anthropic's sample marketplace, as described below.

If a session is already open when you install from the shell, run /reload-plugins in it; otherwise the mod loads next time you start Claude Code. To confirm it loaded, run /plugin; per Anthropic's docs, a dim line under the tabs reads like 1 mod active · token-weather. Built-in mods aren't counted on that line.

To try a mod without installing it, clone its folder and load it for one session:

git clone https://github.com/anthropics/claude-code-playground
claude --plugin-dir ./claude-code-playground/claude-code/mods/token-weather

To keep a sample, add the clone's claude-code/mods folder as a marketplace with /plugin marketplace add ./claude-code-playground/claude-code/mods, then install from claude-code-playground-mods. The marketplace points at your clone, so the mod stops loading if you move or delete that folder.

You need Claude Code 2.1.287 or later in the terminal. The Desktop app bundles its own copy of Claude Code, and Anthropic's overview says mods work there from 2.1.286. Run claude --version to check, and update Claude Code if you're older.

Are Claude Code mods safe?

A mod is exactly as trustworthy as its author: it runs with your permissions, inside Claude Code, and it isn't sandboxed. Anthropic's docs list what an installed mod can do:

  • Read and write files anywhere your account can, start programs and make network requests
  • Read your secrets, including an API key in your environment or settings
  • See every prompt you send and every tool call Claude makes
  • Rewrite a prompt or tool call, or submit a prompt as if you typed it
  • Approve a tool call before you're asked
  • Spend your usage by calling a model on your plan or API key

Sandboxing doesn't help here: it isolates the Bash commands Claude runs, and a process a mod starts runs outside it. Two limits do hold: a mod can't restyle the permission prompt, and where the built-in sec-default guard loads, a user's mod can't approve a call your deny or ask rules would stop. If you rely on auto mode for safety, know that a mod changing a tool call's input after review gets the call denied with a hook changed this call's input after the model wrote it.

Before you install one, read what it does without running it:

claude plugin validate ./some-mod

The hooks: line lists the events it handles and the calls: line every mods API method it calls. A calls: line with $.process.spawn, $.process.run, $.http.fetch or $.fs methods is worth reading the code for: those start programs, reach the network or touch your files.

How do I make my own Claude Code mod?

Easiest: describe it in a Claude Code session, such as make a mod that shows the current git branch above the prompt. Claude uses the built-in plugin-authoring skill, writes the mod under ~/.claude/dev-mods/<session-id>/, and asks whether to turn on hot reloading for the session. In auto and bypassPermissions modes it can load the mod without asking; start in default mode if you want to approve each file. A mod Claude writes only loads in that session, so copy its folder somewhere permanent and load it with --plugin-dir to keep it.

To understand the code, write Anthropic's tutorial mod yourself. I did, on Claude Code 2.1.302 on Windows. It's three files:

first-mod/.claude-plugin/plugin.json, the manifest:

{
  "name": "first-mod",
  "version": "0.1.0",
  "description": "Counts Claude's tool calls, shows the count beside the spinner, and adds a /tally command",
  "author": { "name": "Tahir Nazir" }
}

first-mod/hooks/hooks.json, which points at the code:

{
  "description": "The first-mod hooks module",
  "modules": ["./register.js"]
}

first-mod/hooks/register.js, the hooks module:

let calls = 0

export function register(on) {
  on('session.start', async ($, e, next) => {
    await $.command.register({
      name: 'tally',
      description: 'Show how many tool calls Claude has made',
    })
    return next(e)
  })

  on('tool.call', async ($, e, next) => {
    calls += 1
    $.ui.invalidate('ui.render')
    return next(e)
  })

  on('command.run', { command: 'tally' }, async () => {
    return { text: 'Claude has made ' + calls + ' tool calls since this mod loaded' }
  })

  on('ui.render', { component: 'Spinner' }, async ($, e, next) => {
    return next({ ...e, props: { ...e.props, suffix: ' · tool calls: ' + calls + '…' } })
  })
}

The "modules" key in hooks.json is what makes a plugin a mod. No Node.js, bundler or build step is needed: Claude Code loads .js and .ts files directly.

What validate, test and a headless run printed

claude plugin validate reads the code without running it and lists what Claude Code will see:

  ❯ ./register.js hooks: session.start, tool.call, command.run{command=tally}, ui.render{component=Spinner}
  ❯ ./register.js answers its own command: command.run{command=tally}
  ❯ ./register.js gating hook without .catch: tool.call
  ❯ ./register.js calls: $.command.register, $.ui.invalidate

✔ Validation passed

The gating hook without .catch line is a nudge, not an error: a tool.call hook can refuse calls, and Claude Code wants to know what happens if it fails.

claude plugin test runs a mod's tests with no session, sign-in or network. With Anthropic's sample test (two fake tool calls, then /tally) in tests/first-mod.test.ts:

tests\first-mod.test.ts:
(pass) /tally reports the tool calls the mod has seen [100.48ms]

 1 pass
 0 fail
Ran 1 test across 1 file. [0.47s]

And the command, run headless from PowerShell (no model call, because the mod answers it):

claude -p "/tally" --plugin-dir ./first-mod

first-mod: Claude has made 0 tool calls since this mod loaded

Claude Code puts the mod's name in front of the command's text. On Windows, run that from PowerShell or cmd, not Git Bash: Git Bash rewrites an argument starting with / into a Windows path (MSYS_NO_PATHCONV=1 turns that off).

I didn't run the interactive version. Per Anthropic's tutorial, if you start claude --plugin-dir ./first-mod and ask Claude to do something with a few tool calls, the spinner reads like Thinking · tool calls: 2…, and saving a change to register.js hot-reloads the mod. A reload runs register again, so calls resets to 0.

Why does my Claude Code mod do nothing?

Claude Code skips a mod that fails and carries on, so a broken mod looks like one that does nothing. Run claude plugin validate on its folder first, then claude plugin test, because validate only reads the code. I broke the tutorial mod five ways on 2.1.302 to see what each check says:

What I broke claude plugin validate said
Misspelled event, on('tool.calls', …) "tool.calls" is not an event; $ is always spelled $.noun.event(...) at the call site, on is always on("<event>", hook), and next.to always next.to(e, "<tier>")
Removed "modules" from hooks.json hooks.json must have `hooks` (the hook matchers) or `modules` (hooks modules), or both
Named the plugin claude-tally Plugin name "claude-tally" is reserved: it passes as one of Anthropic's own. A third party's plugin name cannot start with "claude-", "anthropic-", "anthropics-", or "cc-plugin-"…
Wrote const ui = $.ui $.ui is used as a value (a noun of $ bound, passed or read)
Threw an error at load ✔ Validation passed

The last row is the one to remember. Validate passed a mod that crashes the moment it loads; claude plugin test caught it:

(fail) /tally reports the tool calls the mod has seen [97.34ms]
  HooksError: first-mod: hooks module did not load: Error: boom at load

A broken mod's command goes to Claude as a prompt

The headless run of that broken mod showed a trap. stderr printed first-mod: hooks module did not load: Error: boom at load, and then, because /tally no longer existed, Claude Code sent /tally to Claude as an ordinary prompt. Claude looked around the folder and answered with a tally it worked out by hand. That turn used my subscription's usage, and an unattended script would have read Claude's answer as the command's output. Check stderr, or make the command's text something your script can recognize.

Other messages you'll see

Message What it means
hooks module did not load: <reason> The module couldn't load, usually because its top-level code threw. Fix the error named; if it ends the version loaded before is unloaded, run /reload-plugins after fixing
hooks module <name> not loaded: disableAllHooks in managed settings Your organization turned off mods from installed plugins (a debug log line, per Anthropic's troubleshooting page)
installed plugins that are not managed load no hooks module in this mode (--bare) You started with --bare
<event> hook skipped: threw Error: … One hook failed, timed out or returned the wrong shape; the rest of the mod runs
registered /tally but no command.run hook answered it The command exists but no hook answered: wrong matcher, or the hook returned next(e)
was unloaded: it crashed the hooks worker A hook blocked the shared worker thread, for example with a loop that never awaits
No mod loads in a new folder You haven't accepted that folder's trust prompt; start claude there once
Your edits don't take effect You're editing an installed copy; Claude Code runs the cached version. Develop with --plugin-dir

To see whether mods can load at all on your machine, run claude plugin test in a folder with no mod in it. On mine it printed no hooks module to load; there is no hooks/hooks.json naming one in "modules", which, per Anthropic's troubleshooting page, means mods can load. hooks modules are turned off here means a setting blocks them, and the rollout switch served off means Anthropic has turned installed mods off remotely. For everything else, start Claude Code with claude --debug-file ./mod-debug.log --plugin-dir ./your-mod and search the log for your mod's name. If the error isn't about a mod at all, the Claude Code troubleshooting hub lists the rest.

Do mods work in VS Code, the Desktop app and claude -p?

Mod hooks run in the terminal CLI, the Claude Desktop Code tab, the VS Code extension, claude -p, the Agent SDK and cloud sessions, but not in a WSL session of the Desktop app. What a mod draws appears only in the CLI, the Desktop Code tab, and VS Code from extension 2.1.299.

Where you run Claude Code Hooks run Drawings appear
claude in a terminal, including editor terminals and JetBrains Yes Yes
Claude Desktop, Code tab Yes Yes, except terminal-only elements
Claude Desktop, WSL session No (plugins aren't available there) No
VS Code extension chat panel Yes Yes, from extension 2.1.299 (2.1.304 for sessions that skip feature flags, such as Bedrock)
claude -p and the Agent SDK Yes No
Cloud sessions Yes, if the plugin reaches the session No

Hooks also run whichever provider serves the model, including Amazon Bedrock, Google Cloud's Agent Platform (Vertex AI) and Microsoft Foundry.

How do I turn Claude Code mods off?

One mod: disable or uninstall it in the Installed tab of /plugin. Every installed mod for one session: start with claude --safe-mode. Every mod you installed, in every session: set "disableAllHooks": true in ~/.claude/settings.json. That last one also stops your settings hooks and custom status line. None of the three stops built-in mods. If you set CLAUDE_CODE_ENABLE_FUNCTION_HOOKS during early access, remove it: 2.1.287 and later ignore it, so setting it to 0 doesn't keep mods off. My Claude Code settings reference lists where each settings file lives.

Claude Code versions that changed mods

Version Change
2.1.287 (1 Oct 2026) "Added Claude Mods: plugins may now modify deeper behavior"; built-in "You should know" mod
2.1.288 (2 Oct) $.ui.selection(); fixed claude plugin test reporting mods off from a stale saved setting
2.1.289 (3 Oct) Fixed installed mods not loading in the first session after an upgrade; a drawing error no longer ends the session
2.1.290 (5 Oct) claude plugin validate lists each gating hook with whether it has a .catch; mods work for gateway users with no Anthropic account
2.1.292 (6 Oct) prompt.autocomplete event; prompt caching for $.model.complete
2.1.299 (14 Oct) VS Code chat panel draws what mods draw
2.1.323 (12 Nov) Each mod gets its own row above the prompt instead of sharing one drawing
2.1.326 (16 Nov) Mods can use Bash, Read and other tools through $.tool.call in Code Mode (an experimental opt-in from 2.1.323 where Claude writes JavaScript to call its tools); edits in a session's mods folder ask more often

Versions and descriptions are from the changelog and Anthropic's mods docs; dates are npm publish dates. The events and methods still change between releases, so Anthropic's docs say to trust the type files Claude Code writes into your mod's .claude-plugin/types/ folder over any page, this one included.

Key takeaways

  • A Claude Code mod is a plugin whose JavaScript or TypeScript runs inside Claude Code; each hook can observe, rewrite or answer an event.
  • Mods can draw panes and bands, add instant /commands and hold or change tool calls. They arrived in Claude Code 2.1.287 on 1 October 2026.
  • Install with /plugin install name@marketplace, or try one for a session with claude --plugin-dir ./the-mod. Anthropic's samples are token-weather, blast-radius and replay-theater.
  • A mod runs with your permissions and isn't sandboxed. Run claude plugin validate before installing and read its hooks and calls lines.
  • validate only reads the code: on 2.1.302 it passed a mod that throws at load. claude plugin test caught it.
  • When a mod's module fails, its /command reaches Claude as an ordinary prompt, which costs usage and can look like a real answer.

FAQ

Related

  • Claude Code not working? 30+ errors and how to fix them
  • Claude Code auto mode
  • MCP server not showing up in Claude Code
  • Claude Code sandbox
  • Claude Code vs Cursor: how each loads project instructions

FAQ

What are Claude Code mods?

A mod is a Claude Code plugin whose JavaScript or TypeScript runs inside Claude Code. Claude Code calls the mod's functions, called hooks, when an event happens, such as a tool call, a submitted prompt or part of the interface being drawn, and each hook can watch the event, change it, or answer it itself. That lets a mod draw panes and bands, add /commands that run instantly, and hold or rewrite tool calls. Mods arrived in Claude Code 2.1.287 on 1 October 2026.

How do I install a Claude Code mod?

A mod installs like any plugin, from a marketplace: run /plugin install name@marketplace in a session, or claude plugin install name@marketplace in your shell, then /reload-plugins if a session is already open. To try a mod without installing it, clone it and start Claude Code with claude --plugin-dir ./the-mod. Run /plugin and look for the 'mods active' line to confirm it loaded.

Are there official Claude Code mod examples?

Yes. Anthropic shares three sample mods in the claude-code/mods folder of its claude-code-playground repository: token-weather (a context-window forecast above the prompt), blast-radius (holds risky shell commands such as rm -rf and shows what they would change) and replay-theater (a /replay command for the last turn's edits). The source of built-in mods such as /diff and AGENTS.md loading is in the mods folder of the anthropics/claude-code repository.

Are Claude Code mods safe?

Only as safe as their author. A mod runs with your permissions and isn't sandboxed: it can read and write your files, read API keys in your environment and settings, see every prompt and tool call, approve tool calls before you're asked and spend your usage. Before installing one, run claude plugin validate on its folder; the hooks and calls lines list what it handles and what it asks Claude Code to do, without running it.

Why does my Claude Code mod do nothing?

Claude Code skips a mod that fails, so a broken mod looks like one that does nothing. Run claude plugin validate on its folder to catch a misspelled event, a missing modules key or a reserved name, then run claude plugin test, because validate only reads the code and passed a mod that throws when it loads. In a claude -p run the reason goes to stderr, such as 'hooks module did not load: Error: boom at load'.

Do Claude Code mods work in VS Code and the Desktop app?

Yes. Mods run in the CLI, the Code tab of Claude Desktop and the VS Code extension. What a mod draws appears in the VS Code chat panel from extension version 2.1.299. In claude -p and the Agent SDK a mod's hooks run but nothing it draws appears, and in a WSL session of the Desktop app mods don't run at all.

What is the difference between a mod and a hook in Claude Code?

A settings hook is a shell command, HTTP request or prompt you configure in settings.json; it can allow, block or log an event. A mod is code that runs inside Claude Code: it can do the same and also draw in the interface, add instant commands and rewrite events. Anthropic's docs call a mod's handlers hooks too, and the settings-file kind 'settings hooks'.

How do I turn off Claude Code mods?

Disable one mod in the Installed tab of /plugin. To skip every installed mod for one session, start Claude Code with --safe-mode. To stop every mod you installed in every session, set "disableAllHooks": true in ~/.claude/settings.json, which also stops your settings hooks and custom status line. Built-in mods keep running in all three cases.
